Sports.title: Are Arsenal already out of the title race? Ruthless Chelsea expose familiar flaws as Renee Slegers feels the heat after 1-0 derby defeat, writes TARA ANSON-WALSH
Sports.content:
Alyssa Thompson’s first-half strike secured victory for Chelsea in a fierce London derby, as Arsenal’s unbeaten start to the season came to an end.

Katie McCabe was booed throughout the game in an attritional first meeting between the former Arsenal star and her new side.

Ultimately McCabe and her new team-mates had the last laugh, however, with the likes of Lexi Potter and Keira Walsh also starring in midfield in a dominant display for the hosts.

Daily Mail Sport’s women’s football reporter TARA ANSON-WALSH was at Stamford Bridge to give you the things we learned…

Alyssa Thompson’s first-half strike secured victory for Chelsea in a fierce London derby

Are Arsenal out of the title race already?

Much has been said about Arsenal’s lack of goals this season, but the more worrying thing from a fan’s perspective has been the lack of urgency in their play.

Renee Slegers’ side dominated Chelsea for possession and chances in the opening stages of this game, with Kim Little and Mariona Caldentey both hitting the woodwork. But the stats relating to their domination for chances miss the fact that they simply appear off it. Tired, slow, frustrated, lacking confidence.

Nine times out of ten Caldentey would have buried that first-half chance when she broke free and went one-on-one with Hannah Hampton. Alessia Russo meanwhile hasn’t found the back of the net yet this season. It appears Russo has fallen victim to Slegers’ lack of conviction over who should be the starting No 9 between her and Stina Blackstenius, and she hasn’t been allowed to build momentum in either role.

Where the goals are going to come from remains unclear at this stage, as is the injection of conviction that is clearly needed in their press, which appears to have fallen off a cliff.

The passage of play leading up to Chelsea’s winner, where Arsenal were caught off guard playing out from the back and passed up the chance to mop up, summed this up. Ellie Carpenter and Melvine Malard gave the Gunners a lesson in tenacity.

It wasn’t until Chloe Kelly and Caitlin Foord were introduced in the second half that a sense of life was breathed into the Arsenal attack. But by then, it was too late.

The Chelsea players collapsed to the floor at the final whistle, and Sonia Bompastor thumped the air. They looked like they merely wanted it more.

Arsenal are now seventh in the top flight, seven points behind league leaders Manchester City. Historically, the WSL has been decided by notoriously fine margins.

Should Arsenal beat City next weekend, their title race could still be salvaged. But currently that appears to be hanging by the most fragile of threads.

It appears Russo has fallen victim to Slegers’ lack of conviction over who should be the starting No 9 between her and Stina Blackstenius, and she hasn’t been allowed to build momentum

Should there be questions over Slegers?

This all brings us to the question: does Renee Slegers still have what it takes to lead this team forward?

When the 37-year-old was appointed head coach of Arsenal in October 2024, it felt like the squad needed a mental reset. Someone to figuratively wrap an arm around the players after a tense close to Jonas Eidevall’s tenure.

The bounce from Slegers’ injection of positivity and clarity – full back Emily Fox described her as a ‘steadying force’ at the time – was so influential that it carried the Gunners to the Champions League final, which they won.

To say that the fairytale of Lisbon was a one-off for Slegers is harsh, but there are warning signs that her side lack the ruthlessness needed to end their seven-year wait for a league title.

Arsenal had a slow start to the season last campaign, and were eight points behind City by Christmas. Although they only lost the one game all season against the eventual champions, two early draws ultimately proved costly as they fell away early. Likewise, they have dropped seven points this season.

To add to that, Slegers has a sizeable squad full of international starters. Having the likes of Chloe Kelly, Olivia Smith and Caitlin Foord on the bench speaks to a position of privilege, but it appears Slegers is grappling this season with big names, form and how those factors interact. With a World Cup less than a year away, her ability to manage this squad going forward could prove a sticking point.

While it’s certainly too early to call for any decisive changes to be made, the pressure is certainly ramping up.

While it’s certainly too early to call for any decisive changes to be made, the pressure is ramping up on Renee Slegers

Chelsea finally show their teeth

There were multiple questions asked throughout last season about whether Chelsea had lost their winning mentality, with Sonia Bompastor’s side often lacking the ruthless edge to push these tight contests over the line.

In a match which saw clear swings in momentum and tested their defensive resilience, Bompastor’s side stood tall.

‘The plan for us this season is in terms of mindset and mentality, and I think I've been talking a lot about that, to be strong and to be together,’ Bompastor said.

‘I think no matter what happened in the game, I always want to see a group of players, but also a team who is together in our high moments when we are doing well, but also in the low moments.

‘I think we came into this game well prepared in terms of we knew we were going to have some moments in the game where we were probably not in control, especially in possession of the ball.

‘So we prepared the game for those moments to be still moments where we were in control, even if we didn't have the ball, we knew exactly where we wanted to orientate the ball, where we wanted to leave some spaces, and I think we dealt with that really well.

‘We were also really strong in terms of not only mental but also physical aspects. Winning the duels, defending the box, and not conceding against a team with strong attacking talent.’

It’s still early days, but Bompastor’s side showed their bite at Stamford Bridge in a way that was clearly lacking last term, and one that could prove useful for them as they look to reclaim their crown. They certainly look up to the task.

It’s still early days, but Bompastor’s side showed their bite at Stamford Bridge in a way that was clearly lacking last term - while Katie McCabe shone against her former side

A bit of needle is good for the game

The departure of Jonas Eidevall and Emma Hayes were supposed to signal the end of the WSL’s fiercest rivalry, but luckily for the neutral, this fixture hasn’t stopped giving.

Katie McCabe’s transition from red to blue this summer has helped that in no small part. She was given a sign of things to come when she received a chorus of boos while kneeling down to take the team photograph.

The boos followed her every touch throughout the game, while Chelsea fans responded by singing her song with gusto.

As it turned out McCabe had an excellent game, with Sonia Bompastor commending her attitude after the full-time whistle.

‘That’s never easy for a player, who has been there for so many years, to face that club,’ she said. ‘Katie is one of those characters where people boo, that gives her more motivation. I think they probably should have kept quiet.’

More of these, please.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel MUST solve England's defensive crisis if he is to ease pressure on his position - he knows they lack depth but he has to find a fix if he wants to play Premier League-style football, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
While arguing the case for progress on his watch recently, Thomas Tuchel pointed at England’s record in qualifying for the World Cup.

‘Eight wins and no goals conceded,’ Tuchel said. ‘Does that not count?’

It did count, once. But sadly not anymore. The road to World Cup 2026 was indeed smooth for Tuchel in terms of results. But that was against Serbia, Albania, Latvia and Andorra. The problems for England start when they are asked to step up a level.

It irritates Tuchel to be reminded of defeats to top-20 teams such as Senegal, Japan, Argentina and now Spain.

‘You don’t mention that when we beat one,’ was his rather withering point at Wembley on Saturday night.

But the truth is that England’s record of parsimony in 2025 and the early part of 2026 shrinks rather when we consider that his side have now conceded fifteen goals in the last eight games they have played. When the heat has been turned up, England’s back four have melted a little.

And this is perhaps Tuchel’s biggest problem now ahead of a game in Prague on Tuesday night that really must be won if England’s Nations League hopes aren’t to disappear before we have even bought our pumpkins and if pressure slowly building on the German isn’t to crank up a little further.

Thomas Tuchel struggled to find the answers in a tough evening at Wembley against Spain

England have just started a run of four games in 11 days that he knows will test his players physically and he already has a defence on his hands that looks like it needs a lie down after 95 minutes chasing World Champions Spain around Wembley.

If England’s attacking unit broke free from its World Cup chains on Saturday – Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon were particularly excellent – then the likes of Marc Guehi, Jarell Quansah and Nico O’Reilly had nights to forget at the other end of the field.

But what does Tuchel do for Tuesday’s game against Czechia?

Newcastle’s Lewis Hall would, on form, represent an upgrade on O’Reilly at left-back but, that apart, he doesn’t have much wriggle room.

He has little – if any - love for Trent Alexander Arnold’s defensive attributes while his reserve central defenders in this squad are Trevoh Chalobah and Jarrad Branthwaite, who have four caps between them. Oh for Dan Burn, who is injured.

Tuchel acknowledged the problem as he talked late on Saturday night, saying: ‘I would love not to rotate but I am not sure if it’s possible.

‘An ideal scenario would be to go again and go again and go again. With six or seven players minimum from that start again that we trust. To put the responsibility on them and for them to feel the trust. But I am not sure it’s possible. Let’s see.’

Over the course of Tuchel’s two years in charge, so much of the conversation has focused on his use of England’s attacking players.

Nico O'Reilly gave the ball away for Spain's second goal and Lewis Hall may be an upgrade

Is there a problem with Jude Bellingham? Not anymore, gladly. Have we a replacement for Harry Kane? No. Can Phil Foden and Cole Palmer fit in? Not if Saturday’s full throttle, physical approach to attacking football is to be the way.

But it’s across the back that England are starting to feel the pinch. With Harry Maguire in exile, John Stones inching towards the end and Reece James so often injured, England suddenly lack depth and perhaps real world class quality in that area.

At Wembley at half-time against Spain, Kyle Walker was invited on to the pitch to receive thanks for 96 caps of service. The truth is we miss him already and indeed others like him.

England should win in Prague. Czechia have not beaten a team of note since winning against Ukraine two years ago, lost at home to Croatia at the weekend and didn’t hang around at the World Cup longer than the group stages.

Nevertheless, England could do with a performance of real and consistent authority. Not since the second half of their opening World Cup game against Croatia have England looked like a side ready to make the next big step forward.

Tuchel’s team were in such a spot a year ago, too, after a dull 2-0 home win over Andorra in World Cup qualifying. Their response was to go and put five past Serbia in Belgrade.

‘Hopefully we can find that kind of shape and form but if you mean like "do we go for it and try to impose what we did against Spain’ then yes that’s 100 per cent it," said Tuchel.

‘We need to be proactive and go for it. There is no room for managing or an economic style. It’s how the team want to play, how we wanna play so let’s go. It will be a different scenario and setting and a different challenge.’

Kyle Walker was presented with a shirt to mark his 96 caps at half-time on Saturday

If England are now wedded to the Premier League style of football that has been so discussed over the last 10 days then Tuchel must find a way to make them more secure than they were against the world champions.

His assertion that ‘If Harry doesn’t slip with the penalty we win the game’ was reasonable enough. England were in the ascendency at that point and would have gone 3-1 up with Wembley energised.

Equally, Spain would have been 3-0 up within half an hour had they taken straight forward chances. So that’s probably where that game of ifs and buts begins and ends.

This can still be a progressive international break for England. Victories against Czechia (home and away) and behind closed doors in Croatia on Saturday would take Tuchel and his players into November’s games against Croatia and Spain with a shot at winning their Nations League group.

But if Tuchel sounded a little tetchy – by his own laconic standards – on Saturday night, it was not without reason. In the home Euros of 2028, the really big games will need to be won. From that point of view, the search for answers goes on.

Sports.title: Jason Cundy reveals how he became football's most notorious wind-up merchant, the truth behind THAT Ange Postecoglou mask - and insists he will never let up on Spurs foe Jamie O'Hara
Sports.content:
Jason Cundy's public life seems to have one main purpose: to make Jamie O'Hara as miserable and mortified as possible.

Cundy is, by now, football's biggest wind-up merchant. It is a role he revels in, and one which has brought talkSPORT's Sports Bar show immense popularity on social media.

He is in his element with that ridiculous Ange Postecoglou mask stretched comically over his head, firing wisecracks and shameful stats about Tottenham over at O'Hara, who can only sit with his head in his hands and take the mockery.

So, how much pleasure does Cundy take in tearing his radio co-pilot to shreds?

'A huge amount,' he tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I don't feel for Jamie.

'Every single game, they lose or manage not to score. Never has the expression 'the gift that keeps giving' been more appropriate to Spurs at any other time.'

Jason Cundy has become football's biggest wind-up merchant due to Tottenham's decline

His Ange Postecoglou mask and jibes have been a menace to talkSPORT co-host Jamie O'Hara

Cundy even turned up to O'Hara's wedding wearing the mask and takes 'huge' pleasure in annoying him

There is something relentlessly funny about the Postecoglou mask. Something about the sheer smugness of it, the expressionlessness, as O'Hara sits a metre away having meltdown after meltdown as this warped face just... watches him, unblinking.

O'Hara couldn't even escape the haunting face at his wedding to Keziah Grubb this year. On one of the biggest days of O'Hara's life, there was Cundy, head wrapped tight in his favourite Postecoglou-themed plaything.

In the week after our interview, Cundy posts no fewer than eight clips of him ripping into O'Hara's former club Tottenham, who are bottom of the Premier League and winless. In one, he diagnoses the club with 'Spursitis', something nobody in football wants.

TalkSPORT has often fallen foul of accusations of ragebaiting its listeners too much, but the mask is almost universally loved by its viewers on social media – unless they're Tottenham fans.

'I came up with the idea to get masked because talkSPORT is so visual,' Cundy says. 'I didn't realise it would take on a whole life of its own.

'We bought them from South America and we order a new mask every year.

'We bought the Ange mask when he was the manager at Nottingham Forest, and by the time the mask turned up he'd got sacked, so I had to find a role for it.

'We've got a Gary Neville one, an Arne Slot one, and now we've got a Jamie Carragher one, that'll come out soon.

Cundy was speaking to Daily Mail Sport on behalf of TENA Men, which was sponsoring the 2026 Prostate United launch event

'It's the same mask each time. It absolutely stinks! It's got a weird smell about it. I tell Jamie it's the smell of failure. That's what it stinks of.

'I did clean it but think it's best to just leave it now, just to do what it does, somehow just let it lie in its own stink, and the worse the mask gets the worse Spurs get.'

Cundy was speaking to Daily Mail Sport on behalf of TENA Men, who were sponsoring the 2026 Prostate United launch event. The 56-year-old is a survivor of testicular cancer, so the issue of men's health is close to his heart.

'I have a voice to speak and spread a message - go and get yourself checked for testicular cancer, or get a PSA check. You have a duty to yourself and your family.'

He has brought his cancer experience onto the airwaves before, recording a long-form interview with talkSPORT on the subject in 2022, showing a deeper, more sensitive side to his personality than the joker we typically get to hear.

There is a pitfall in the show's reliance on Spurs being bad: namely, what if the north Londoners start being good?

Maybe O'Hara would then have the chance to turn the tables on his mate and have a dig at his alma mater Chelsea.

In any case, Cundy isn't too worried about Tottenham becoming sensations overnight.

Tottenham are bottom of the table and winless this season under manager Roberto De Zerbi

'You can't finish 17th, 17th, and go into a new season expecting there to be a huge dramatic change,' he says.

'Spurs aren't in the big six. Spurs would be in the big six in the Championship if they're not too careful.

'If they carry on being c***, Roberto De Zerbi will get the sack. That's football. That goes for every manager, not just him. But because it's Spurs, history is repeating itself.

'They've signed players that don't score goals: Omar Marmoush scored eight last season, Savio four. Mathys Tel, meh, four. Richarlison's not in the Premier League squad.

'If you put Erling Haaland up top, he still wouldn't score. They don't create chances.'

Jason Cundy was speaking on behalf of TENA Men, who sponsored the 2026 Prostate United launch event. To find out more about Prostate Cancer UK’s football fundraising challenge visit – prostateunited.prostatecanceruk.org

Sports.title: Man United hit with injury scares as captain Bruno Fernandes is ruled out of Portugal clash with 'complicated problem'... and Patrick Dorgu is taken off early playing for Denmark
Sports.content:
Manchester United are braced for a double injury blow with captain Bruno Fernandes ruled out of Portugal's Nations League clash with Norway on Sunday and Denmark's Patrick Dorgu forced off early against Wales. Fernandes, 32, was substituted late on in in Thursday's 1-0 win over Wales in Lisbon and manager Jorge Jesus has confirmed he will play no part in Oslo - as well as claiming he has played through pain in recent games for United. 'In the game against Wales, we went in with all the available players but Bruno Fernandes came off with a complicated problem,' said Jesus. Jesus added: 'He said he’s been dealing with that pain for about three games, and that was one of the factors that prevented him from being at his usual level against Wales. 'He was my player, I know him perfectly. I’ve already spoken to him. I prefer not to risk him in this game and have him clean and in good physical condition for the Denmark game (in Copenhagen on Thursday).' His absence means the midfielder will be denied a second clash with Erling Haaland this month, having suffered a 1-0 defeat in the Manchester derby at Old Trafford which saw the Norway striker score the only goal. Bruno Fernandes featured in the 1-0 win against Wales but was forced off late on Dorgu, meanwhile, was substituted after going down just 30 minutes into Denmark's clash with Wales in Copenhagen. Any serious injury would add to United's worries, with Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo both withdrawing from England’s squad and forward Benjamin Sesko recovering from a shin issue that has seen him miss Slovenia's internationals this month. But the club will be most concerned about Fernandes, who has played 90 minutes in all five of United Premier League matches so far this season as well as the entirety of their 4-0 Champions League win over Sabah. He was also brought off the bench in an attempt to rescue his side after they blew a two-goal lead at home to Brighton in the Carabao Cup. United return to action on Saturday October 10, at home to Tottenham. They have endured a frustrated start to the season under Michael Carrick with their sole Premier League win coming against Ipswich - in which they needed a Fernandes hat-trick to secure a 5-2 victory.

Sports.title: Tom Banton's blistering 126 ends difficult English summer on a high with crushing win over Sri Lanka... as happy captain Harry Brook revels in 'near-perfect' display
Sports.content:
Tom Banton's blistering 126 ends difficult English summer on a high with crushing win over Sri Lanka... as happy captain Harry Brook revels in 'near-perfect' display

England’s long – and at times difficult – summer ended on a high as a maiden international century for Tom Banton set up a crushing 223-run win over Sri Lanka.

There were runs too for Jordan Cox, who hit a sparkling 76 off 52 balls as Jos Buttler’s injury replacement, plus a contender for the ball of the season from Sonny Baker, who found Pathum Nissanka’s outside edge in the second over of the chase with an unplayable delivery that swung and took off as if from a trampoline.

Above all, England were able to breathe more freely after blowing their run-chase at Headingley on Thursday, a meltdown which raised the possibility that the white-ball progress made under Harry Brook might be undermined at the last.

Instead, Brook – who contributed a typically effervescent 77 – could celebrate a third successive ODI series win, England’s first such sequence since 2023, when their opponents included Bangladesh and Ireland. Since replacing Buttler as captain last year, he has presided over 33 white-ball victories and only 11 defeats, with England’s T20 form especially hot.

But the next World Cup, starting in southern Africa in just over a year’s time, is a 50-over affair, and Brook must be quietly thrilled not only that the talk is once more about the actual cricket rather than off-field misadventure, but that options are starting to emerge after some fallow years for the one-day team.

Banton is chief among them, having taken his chance to stand in for the injured Jacob Bethell with aplomb. After making 73 three days earlier, he looked in no mood to miss out on three figures, using his height and power to launch five sixes in a blistering 105-ball 126 that will ensure Bethell’s return is no gimme.

"Beauty from Sonny Baker!"



What a start for England 🔥 pic.twitter.com/wLQ9R6J2pv — Sky Sports Cricket (@SkyCricket) September 27, 2026

Tom Banton hit a series of superb boundaries in his innings of 126 as England posted 355-7

Banton was able to celebrate his first century in style as he helped England to a series win

His first six, an uppercut off Dilshan Madushanka, showed off his hand-eye coordination. Later, he pulled Madushanka for six more, then deposited his next ball over long-off with exquisite timing.

‘To get over the line is a feeling I can’t explain,’ said Banton. ‘There are times when you’re sat there in your room wondering if that chance with England will ever come again. It’s been an amazing day.’

All the while, Brook was moving through the gears after a sticky start against the left-arm spin of Dunith Wellalage. After labouring to 10 off 24 balls, including a bad drop at wide slip by Nissanka on seven, he smashed 67 off his next 42, before slapping seamer Asitha Fernando to mid-off.

It meant Brook finished the international summer with 10 scores of at least 50 from 23 innings, but only one century. And yet his cross-format average is 50, and his strike-rate 114 – remarkable when you consider 11 of those innings have been in Tests. Ominously for opponents, it feels as if there is room for improvement.

The icing on England’s cake was provided by Cox. As Bethell’s stand-in at No 3 in the Test side, he took three half-centuries off Pakistan. Here, he made light of Buttler’s absence as 104 came from the last 10 overs. Until now, Cox’s ODI career had consisted of three underwhelming appearances in the Caribbean in late 2024. He had not made a one-day fifty of any kind. On this evidence, he looks hard to ignore.

‘I thought that was near perfect,’ said Brook. ‘Everyone chipped in beautifully. We’re building towards a squad where, if someone does go down, someone else can come in and perform. Coxy was exceptional, and I was really proud of the way Bants played.’

It was a less fruitful day for two more experienced players. Ben Duckett was bowled for a duck by a beauty from Madushanka, while Joe Root made just 18 before he fell lbw to Janith Liyanage. Of his 13 dismissals in the three international formats this season, nine have been leg-before.

Harry Brook capped off an eventful cricketing summer on a high with a 2-1 series victory

For only the second time in his career, he has gone through a home summer without a hundred for either England or Yorkshire. Since the only other instance came in 2020, when Covid limited him to 11 knocks for England and none at all for his county, 2026 is very much the outlier.

Sri Lanka had never knocked off more than 322, so a target of 357 looked beyond them even before the irrepressible Baker undid Nissanka and celebrated his first ODI wicket with a characteristic leap and punch of the air.

Gus Atkinson bounced out both Mendises – Kamindu and Kushal – and Jofra Archer’s direct hit did for Pavan Rathnayake. Cox had dislodged the bails with his gloves before the ball arrived, but the fact that Archer’s deadeye throw uprooted the stump meant Cox’s blunder went unpunished.

The rest was a procession, with Liam Dawson – preferred to Rehan Ahmed – hoovering up three wickets, and Sri Lanka were all out for 132 with more than 20 overs of their innings unused. An anti-climax, perhaps, but England weren’t complaining.

Sports.title: Jude Bellingham only knows how to play one way - he and England must embrace it
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel says Jude Bellingham is at his best when he plays with “fire and rage.”

In fact, England boss Tuchel says it is the only way Bellingham knows how to play. And it is definitely the only way England know how to play.

Real Madrid superstar Bellingham was sensational against Spain and he actually got better and stronger as the game wore on.

England had the beating of Spain when it was high intensity, chaotic and fast. Spain came out on top because they remained calm, rode their luck and showed their experience and quality.

‌



But if any one player showed England can compete with the best then it was Bellingham. And despite being an absolute world superstar with Real Madrid, some of his best qualities are English.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

“It’s the only style he can play, that’s just his game,” said Tuchel who said he thrived on the atmosphere, occasion and even his Real Madrid team mate Marc Cucurella trying to wind him up.

‌



“He likes that. He gets better if that happens. It’s better if he plays with a bit of rage. It’s what he does. I think sometimes he is looking for these moments to get his fire going.

“I think he doesn’t know any team-mates on the national team. He wants to win. He doesn’t know any team-mates. He is still friends with them but not for the 90 minutes.”

Bellingham was strong throughout, providing the assist for Antony Gordon’s equaliser. He also won the penalty which Harry Kane missed after slipping. In injury time, his fierce shot nearly brought another equaliser.

This was World Cup Jude at Wembley. He is still only 23 and can become England’s most capped player of all time and the best player in the nation’s history.

‌



View 4 Images Thomas Tuchel was full of praise for Bellingham

But Bellingham only knows how to play one way and, despite Tuchel insisting that he will not rest and rotate, it is unlikely that even England’s midfield master will be able to complete four lots of 90 minutes in the space of 11 days.

Tuchel says there is a big difference between 70 minutes and 90 because the last 20 is generally when players get injured.

Tuchel warned: “He doesn’t play an economic game but let’s see. I would love to have him four times on the pitch. I think the concern is that he hasn’t done it this season in this tight period. We will need to check with the physios. We will not put Jude at any risk. But is style is how he plays.”

‌



And make no mistake, Bellingham - and Kane - would get into this Spain team. Gordon played really well and might push Nico Williams.

The point is the gap is closing but it is not because England have suddenly changed their DNA and play better football like Spain. Spain’s success would suggest their style is better. But England cannot suddenly reinvent themselves. That is for future generations.

View 4 Images England had world champions Spain on the ropes, but ultimately fell short

England did go toe-to-toe with the world champions and had the beating of them when they were playing their brand of chaotic, high intensity football.

‌



Spain were controlled, brilliant and showed their quality because they never panicked even when they were 2-1 down and under the cosh.

That was the difference. Along with one Harry Kane slip from a missed penalty to make it 3-1. England were shocking defensively. They made so many errors.

England’s defence was not good enough at the World Cup. And it is still an issue. They could have gone 4-0 down. James Trafford was a positive on his big audition.

View 4 Images Harry Kane's missed penalty was the turning point at Wembley (Image: Rob Newell - CameraSport via Getty Images)

‌



Nico O’Reilly and Marc Guehi both made big mistakes which led to goals with Lamine Yamal, Alex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal on target. Maybe the Manchester City pair were distracted by the seismic events with their club under threat from Premier League charges. They looked it.

Kane made it 86 goals from 122 caps to put England ahead. And at 2-1 up, England were so in control. Spain were overwhelmed. Kane’s miss was a moment which cost England.

Tuchel added: “If Harry doesn’t slip we win the game. You can have a different point of view but from mine if Harry doesn’t slip we go two goals up. We were clearly the better team until that moment in the second half and we win that game.

“But even if we had won we would have deserved it but it wouldn’t have made us favourites for the Euros. We need to go step by step. They came with the strongest team I think.

‌



“We had some key players missing. I am fine with this performance. We could have won the game and didn’t. I have told you the reasons and that’s it.”

Sports.title: Liverpool suffer another injury blow as Cody Gakpo hurt on international duty
Sports.content:
Liverpool suffer another injury blow as Cody Gakpo hurt on international duty

Cody Gakpo was forced off with an injury just 17 minutes into the Netherlands' clash with Serbia in the Nations League, providing Liverpool with another scare during the international break

View 2 Images Cody Gakpo has picked up an injury (Image: ANP via Getty Images)

Liverpool have been dealt a second injury blow in a matter of hours after Cody Gakpo had to be substituted for the Netherlands. Gakpo, 27, signalled to come off in the 17th minute of Sunday's game away to Serbia after being on the end of two strong challenges in quick succesion.

‌



The forward had scored for his country last time out to earn a 1-1 draw with Germany on Thursday, continuing a hot streak of form. But Gakpo's productive start to the season could be halted by the injury, having limped off the pitch during the Nations League fixture.

‌



Netherlands boss Xavi Hernandez is expected to provide an update at full-time. Earlier on Sunday, Liverpool discovered that Alexander Isak had picked up a thigh injury while playing for Sweden.

‌



The striker has now left Sweden's camp and will miss their three remaining matches. Although Liverpool don't return to action until October 11 against Manchester City, Reds boss Andoni Iraola will likely be sweating over his team selection already.

‌



Gakpo and Isak have already combined for four goals this season, including their 1-0 win at Bournemouth prior to the international break. Sweden boss Graham Potter explained the nature of Isak's injury in a press conference before their match at home to Poland on Monday.

"He's got a small problem with his thigh," Potter said. "It's not a big one but because of the amount of games we've got in a small space of time, he won't be able to make those.

"Not a big one but it's frustrating for him and obviously for us. It is what it is but we move forward with the players we have.

‌



"It was during the game. Like anything, you sometimes get bumps and bruises in the game, you might think it's a bit of a dead leg or something. But actually as the 24 hours, 48 hours after the game, not quite what you think.

How should Liverpool line up if Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak are missing? Let us know your XI in the comments section.

View 2 Images Cody Gakpo was tackled by Serbia's Sasa Lukic (Image: Roy Lazet/Soccrates/Getty Images)

‌



"Unfortunately after getting it checked out, it's a little bit more than what you think during the match. He has to miss the rest of the camp.

"Our medical team has been in contact with the club. Obviously it's our decision in the first place because of his status, in terms of his injury. Once that's the case, we have to inform everybody. That's just normal.

"We've got a really big squad that we believe in. Clearly there's not another Alexander Isak, that's obvious.

Article continues below

"In an ideal world, we want all our players available but the reality is we don't have Alex for this game… clearly whoever comes in, we're not going to ask them to be Alex. They just need to be themselves in the best way they can."

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel has failed his main England task and Spain defeat felt inevitable
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel’s England have played three matches at Wembley in 2026 and have not recorded a victory. They have been beaten by Japan and Spain and have drawn against Uruguay.

It continues to be a small wonder that Wembley is packed for every international. It will probably be close to full for the visit of the Czech Republic on Tuesday week.

To be fair, the 84,525 who showed up for the UEFA Nations League game against Spain were treated to a highly entertaining contest and an extended look at the wonder of Lamine Yamal.

But they heard familiar reflections from Tuchel. England could have won the game had certain moments gone their way.

‌



If my aunt had … etc, etc. You get the drift.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

The England manager suggested his side would have gone on to win had Harry Kane extended their one-goal lead from the penalty spot early in the second half, and, quite obviously, he has a point.

‌



But the Kane miss averts scrutiny of the gap in class between the two squads.

The statistics showed that Spain were marginally the more threatening side in a game that could have ended up with double its five-goal tally. The eyes showed that Spain were comfortably the more accomplished side.

England managed to win a knockabout bronze medal match against France at the World Cup but are generally found wanting against high-class opposition.

View 2 Images Tuchel's England fell short against world champions Spain

‌



Tuchel was brought in to change that. He hasn’t. Spain could have been out of sight before Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane led England’s impressive resurgence.

And it was impressive. Gordon was a constant threat and Jude Bellingham was at his belligerent best.

But there was a feeling of inevitability about the defeat. It is why punters were heading for the tube station some time before the final whistle.

It is why England’s lap of appreciation went pretty much unnoticed. There was an indifference to Tuchel on Saturday night and that will be the case all the way to the Euro finals.

‌



A victory over the world champions might - just might - have changed that, but the cold truth is that Tuchel failed in his original brief yet is still the manager entrusted to take England forward.

The fantastic attendances at Wembley are all the Football Association needs to be convinced their decision to keep the England team in Tuchel’s hands is the right one. And a slightly cavalier and error-prone display against the Spanish certainly made the latest game value for money.

But even if you did not agree with the move to have a third foreign manager in charge of the England national team, Tuchel’s initial short-term, win-or-bust mission had a frisson of excitement about it.

‌



There was in-game excitement against Spain, that is for sure. But there was also a familiarity about being second best against quality opposition - and an acceptance that Tuchel is unlikely to change that.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland beat Israel in controversial Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
