Former President George M. Weah, political leader, Congress for Democratic Change (CDC)

The Sunday gathering follows two meetings held earlier this month.

The first, on September 5, brought together a broader group of opposition stakeholders, while a second meeting on September 6 focused specifically on political leaders of opposition parties.

Those engagements, according to the statement, provided an opportunity for the participants to discuss Liberia’s national situation, identify areas of common interest and explore possible avenues for cooperation.

The September 27 meeting is expected to focus more specifically on the practical side of that cooperation, including structures, mechanisms and other arrangements intended to sustain the consultations.

Alexander Benedict Cummings, political leader, Alternative National Congress (ANC).

Beyond an Electoral Alliance

The opposition leaders say their discussions are not being framed solely around the possibility of an electoral alliance.

Instead, they say the emerging cooperation is intended to provide a platform for collective consideration of Liberia’s national challenges and the development of practical responses.

“The Opposition Political Leaders remain firmly committed to sustaining the foundation of opposition unity, not merely as a means towards an electoral alliance,” the statement said, adding that the process is also intended to promote “collective ideas, constructive engagement, and practical solutions” in the interest of Liberians.

Amb. Dee Maxwell Saah Kemayah, political leader and standard bearer, Movement for Economic Empowerment (MOVEE)

The proposed Joint Communiqué is expected to document the understandings reached during the consultations and establish a basis for continued engagement among the participating parties.

The communiqué is scheduled to be signed publicly at the conclusion of Sunday’s roundtable.

The initiative comes as opposition parties continue consultations over possible areas of cooperation ahead of Liberia’s next electoral cycle.

Jonathan A. Mason, political leader, Union of Liberian Democrats Party (ULDP)

The parties have yet to publicly announce a common political ticket or broader electoral arrangement, and Sunday’s meeting is being presented by the technical committee as part of an ongoing process of consultation and coordination.

The Opposition Political Parties Joint Technical Committee issued the statement on behalf of the participating parties.

World.title: Liberia: Women Have Not Had Central Role in  War Crimes Court Preparations; A New Project Wants to Change That
World.content:
Women and children carry their belongings through heavy rain near Stockton Bridge in Monrovia in 2003 fleeing fighting between forces loyal to then President Charles Taylor and rebels of the Liberians United for Reconciliation and Democracy (LURD). Photo: Chris Hondros/Getty Images.

Women have not played a major visible role in recent efforts for postwar justice despite being key targets of much of the violence of the war years. A new project aims to change that by strengthening women’s groups and bringing more women, including young women, into peacebuilding and justice discussions.

Women leaders say they have been discouraged from coming forward to play a more central role in the process by harassment and attacks.

Leaders of the US$3 million project headed by say women should not be seen only as victims of the civil wars. They should also lead investigations, prosecutions, reparations and other parts of the justice, reconciliation and commemoration process.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

More than two decades after Liberian women helped played a decisive role in bringing the country’s civil wars to an end, they have been far less visible in the renewed push to reckon with the wars’ atrocities committed during them.

No woman was shortlisted to lead the Office of the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court of Liberia, and many of the major groups shaping the process are headed by men. Women are involved — including in senior positions and through women-led organizations — but they have been less prominent in some of the key leadership and decision-making spaces.



Women leaders have told FrontPage Africa/New Narratives that they have been reluctant to speak up on the postwar justice process because of attacks and belittling that they have been subjected to in the past.

A new US$3 million initiative is seeking to boost women’s involvement. The project, called the “Gender Promotion Initiative 2.0,” rolled out last week by the Liberian government, the United Nations, Kvinna till Kvinna and other partners, aims to strengthen women’s organizations and bring more women, including young women, into peacebuilding and justice discussions. The three-year project will be implemented in Montserrado, Lofa, Nimba, Grand Gedeh and Grand Cape Mount. The United Nations says more than 40 percent of its resources will go directly to women’s rights organizations.

Mabel M.K. Kear, programme manager at Kvinna till Kvinna, called the initiative “a critical promise that the sacrifices of women and communities will lead to transformation,” adding that reconciliation should be genuine and “peace will be sustained through justice.”

More than 250,000 people were killed during Liberia’s 14 years of civil conflict, according to the United Nations . A 2016 United Nations human rights report said 1.5 million people were displaced inside Liberia or sought refuge in other countries. The report cited a 2005 estimate that 75 percent of Liberian women and girls were subjected to wartime rape.

Liberia’s 2009 Truth and Reconciliation Commission concluded that “women were singled out for abuse simply on account of their gender.” It also found that forced displacement “took a particularly heavy toll on women,” many of whom became heads of their families after losing their spouses.

But women were also central to in ending the fighting. Christian and Muslim women joined forces through the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace, staging protests, prayer meetings and other nonviolent actions and taking their demands for peace to negotiations in Accra, Ghana. It was there that they staged a daring threat to undress. This was a cultural signal that the men could not ignore. They swiftly brought the negotiations to a successful conclusion. Leymah Gbowee, as one of the group’s leaders, was later awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for their actions.

Liberian women demanding peace in Monrovia —2003. Credit: Pewee Flomoku.

Asatu Bah Kenneth, was one of those leaders fighting for the end of the war in 2003. Today she is the most senior woman working in the court process as the director of the Office of War and Economic Crimes Anti-Corruption Division. Kenneth also founded and led the Liberia Muslim Women for Peace, which joined the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace, whose sustained nonviolent campaign helped pressure Liberia’s warring parties toward peace in 2003.

Women-led groups, including the Female Lawyers Association of Liberia and the Women’s NGO Secretariat of Liberia, are also involved in the current justice process.

That history returned to the international stage this week. The Liberian government held a high-level event on women, peace and security at United Nations headquarters in New York on the margins of the 81st United Nations General Assembly, celebrating women’s historic role in the country’s peace process while calling for greater leadership by women and girls. The event, organized by the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, was held under the theme “From Pioneers to Global Leaders: Liberia’s Journey in Women, Peace and Security.”

President Joseph Boakai used the event to link that legacy to women’s participation in justice today. Launching Liberia’s third National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security, he identified participation and access to justice among its priorities and reaffirmed his commitment to establishing the War and Economic Crimes Court. Boakai used the event to highlight women’s role in national decision-making.

“In Liberia, men make the big decisions, the women make the small decisions, but the women decide which decisions are big and which decisions are small,” Boakai said.

Nobel Peace laureate Leymah Gbowee, who helped lead the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace, used the same event to recall how women organized and pushed for peace despite initially being excluded from important spaces.

“Contrary to popular belief that we were a bunch of women who had no strategic direction, we had a direction,” Gbowee said.

Government militia fighters advance during fighting for control of a key bridge in Monrovia in 2003, as forces loyal to President Charles Taylor battled rebels of the Liberians United for Reconciliation and Democracy (LURD). Photo: Chris Hondros

The renewed focus on women’s participation comes at a pivotal stage in the effort to establish the court. Boakai submitted legislation to establish the War and Economic Crimes Court and a National Anti-Corruption Court to the Legislature in May. Weeks earlier, he had renewed the mandate of the Office for the Establishment of a War and Economic Crimes Court of Liberia .

The Legislature is considering competing proposals from the Liberian National Bar Association, a civil society coalition led by the Independent National Commission on Human Rights, as well as Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah .

For supporters of the new gender initiative, the challenge is ensuring that women have a greater role as those decisions are made.

Christine N. Umutoni, the United Nations resident coordinator in Liberia, said the initiative should build on a voice Liberian women have already established rather than treat their participation as something new.

“Liberian women helped end the conflict,” Umutoni said. “So it is not now that we are building the voice.”

The challenge, she said, is ensuring that women’s experiences are reflected throughout the justice process. She warned that “a gender-blind approach would leave serious violations insufficiently addressed and risk weakening public confidence in justice institutions.”

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Rep. Jacob Debee Receiving Treatment at Phebe Hospital After Road Accident in Bong County
World.content:
SUAKOKO DISTRICT –Grand Gedeh County’s District Three lawmaker, Representative Jacob Debee, is currently hospitalized after being involved in a road accident along a stretch of highway in Gbondoi Town, located in Yellequelleh District, Bong County.

Following the incident, the legislator was transported to Phebe Hospital in Suakoko District for medical attention, where he remains under care.

Witnesses at the scene say Rep. Debee was en route to the southeastern region of the country at the time of the crash. He was driving a white Toyota Land Cruiser, registration number A-613397, when the vehicle is said to have run off the roadway. Early indications suggest no other vehicle was involved.



It has not yet been confirmed how serious Rep. Debee’s injuries are, nor whether anyone else was riding with him when the accident happened.

As of this report, the Liberia National Police have not released an official account of the crash. Updates are expected once investigators complete their assessment.

World.title: YEIB-MANCO Targets 30,000 Liberian Youth, Moves to Tackle Credit Barriers
World.content:
Monrovia — The Youth Entrepreneurship and Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO) is targeting at least 30,000 young Liberians for direct support and another 120,000 indirectly, as it rolls out a financing model aimed at addressing some of the major barriers confronting local entrepreneurs, including high interest rates, stringent collateral requirements and limited access to long-term credit.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

YEIB-MANCO Chief Executive Officer Joseph F. Sando disclosed the targets Thursday during an engagement with journalists in Monrovia, where he outlined the institution’s mandate, financing structure and plans to expand entrepreneurship opportunities across Liberia.



Sando described YEIB-MANCO as a multifunctional institution established through an African Development Bank-backed initiative with the Government of Liberia, with the Ministry of Commerce and Industry serving as a key institutional anchor.

“When anyone hears the word YEIBMANCO, the thing that should register to the mind is sustainable development, sustainable economic development for our country, Liberia, and by extension, Africa,” Sando said.

Despite the word “bank” in its name, Sando said YEIB-MANCO is designed to go beyond traditional lending by combining financing with business development, technical assistance and incubation services.

“It’s a combination of many companies that carry the weight of development in finance, business and incubation,” he said.

Beyond Lending

Sando said YEIB-MANCO remains in its formative stage, with about six people directly working for the institution and nearly 15 when personnel connected to the project implementation structure are included.

However, he said its mandate is nationwide, with a particular focus on young people and women.

Responding about how ordinary Liberians would benefit, Sando said the initiative is designed to reach entrepreneurs across all 15 counties rather than concentrate opportunities in Monrovia.

“To me, in my heart, there is no ordinary Liberian. Everybody in Liberia is an exceptional, extraordinary person,” he said.

According to Sando, beneficiaries will not simply receive financing based on business ideas. Prospective entrepreneurs will first undergo incubation, training and coaching to assess their capabilities and identify sectors where their businesses have the strongest potential.

“You prepare the businessman in all sectors, especially agriculture, and then you take them to the next stage of financing. You give them money,” he said.

“So you’re not just coming to give money to somebody who tells you, ‘Yeah, I can do business.’ You’re preparing and you’re teaching them, you’re coaching them as to how to go about doing the business.”

After financing, Sando said YEIBMANCO would continue monitoring and evaluating beneficiaries and their businesses to assess performance and economic impact.

Three-Pronged Financing Model

Sando said the institution plans to operate through three special-purpose vehicles covering technical assistance and business development services, a guarantee fund and an investment fund.

Under the business development component, entrepreneurs would undergo incubation designed to identify their skills, business interests and appropriate sectors.

The guarantee mechanism, he said, would involve partnerships with commercial banks to address major financing obstacles facing Liberian entrepreneurs, particularly high interest rates, demanding collateral requirements and short repayment periods.

YEIBMANCO could share financing risks with participating financial institutions, Sando said, potentially reducing the collateral burden on entrepreneurs while helping negotiate more favorable interest rates and longer repayment periods.

He illustrated the difficulty faced by entrepreneurs who may be required to provide collateral worth substantially more than the amount they seek to borrow.

“But if I had that money, I wouldn’t come here,” he said.

The investment component would focus on direct coaching and financing in sectors including agriculture, light manufacturing, logistics, technology and recreation.

Sando said the broader objective is to encourage more Liberians to pursue entrepreneurship and reduce heavy dependence on government employment.

He argued that sustainable private businesses could help ease pressure on the public sector, where large numbers of job seekers compete for limited government positions while personnel costs consume significant public resources.

Demand Outpaces Pilot Capacity

Sando said early demand for YEIBMANCO’s business development program has already demonstrated the scale of interest among young Liberians.

According to him, the institution launched a pilot call for applications in August seeking 50 participants for business development services training.

Within the first week, about 300 people had applied, with applications subsequently exceeding 640 for the 50 available slots.

“That tells you how much young people are there outside there waiting, just for that or something to trigger to see how they can go after their success,” Sando said.

He said teams have also been dispatched to Grand Bassa, Nimba and Margibi counties to engage prospective beneficiaries and verify businesses rather than relying solely on documents submitted by applicants.

Sando stressed that transparency and verifiable data would be central to the initiative, saying journalists and the public should eventually be able to independently confirm beneficiaries and businesses supported under the program.

“We want our people to go and interview the beneficiaries, so that tomorrow you people who understand the watchdog, when you come in, we have the data and data is provable,” he said.

$1.03 Billion Financing Gap

On financing, Sando said initial support is coming from the African Development Bank but argued that considerably greater investment will eventually be required to build a vibrant and sustainable micro, small and medium enterprise sector in Liberia.

He cited approximately US$1.03 billion as the level of financing he believes would ultimately be required to strengthen Liberia’s MSME sector, while acknowledging that current resources remain far below that figure.

“So bringing maybe US$10 million, US$15 million, US$20 million, that’s just a drop of water in a mighty ocean,” Sando said. “However, we’re encouraged that at least we have something to start with.”

He said YEIBMANCO is targeting no fewer than 30,000 young people for direct support, with approximately 120,000 expected to benefit indirectly.

While the initiative places particular emphasis on people between ages 18 and 35 and women, Sando said older business owners would not automatically be excluded.

He said businesses owned by older Liberians could qualify if young people constitute about 60% to 70% of their workforce or occupy significant management positions.

The approach, he said, is intended to support not only businesses owned by young people but also enterprises capable of creating meaningful employment and leadership opportunities for them.

Sando thanked the African Development Bank and Liberian government officials and institutions involved in establishing the initiative, saying their collaboration helped create the foundation for the program.

For Sando, the broader ambition is to build businesses capable of creating jobs, generating sustainable incomes and reducing young Liberians’ dependence on government employment.

“We have taken on the challenge that we will lead our people to making sure Liberia becomes second to none in economic development,” Sando said.

World.title: Liberia: Former Ganta Mayor Suah Faces Court Summons Amid Escalating Feud with Chief Justice Gbeisay Over Nimba Land Row
World.content:
GOMPA, Nimba County — A bitter property dispute in Gompa City has widened into a direct clash between the judiciary and local politics, after the Gompa Magisterial Court issued a summons for former Mayor Amos N. G. Suah in connection with remarks he made about Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Court officials moved to summon Suah after he issued pointed criticism of the Chief Justice’s role in overseeing the disputed land matter, including comments that questioned why Gbeisay had inserted himself into property affairs in Nimba County.



Tensions escalated further when Gbeisay took to the airwaves to defend a controversial eviction and demolition operation carried out in Gompa. He insisted the action stemmed strictly from a magisterial court order and did not represent the Supreme Court acting on its own initiative.

More than 15 households were displaced when structures were torn down or residents were forced out, according to accounts of the operation. Many of those affected have complained that they were given inadequate notice, even as the underlying ownership questions remain legally unsettled.

The case driving the evictions centers on land tied to the estate of the late Musa Toure, pursued through administrator Mohammed Toure against defendants Mohammed Bility and a second individual known as Mr. Dorley. Families connected to the Toure estate contend they have lived on and improved the property for upward of twenty years, arguing that sustained occupation should carry weight against rival paper claims to the land.

The conflict took a sharper political turn when the Chief Justice, during his radio remarks, alleged that Suah had improperly sold public land to private buyers while serving as mayor of Ganta. Gbeisay went on to claim that former Nimba County Superintendent David Door Cooper and the late Senator Prince Yormie Johnson were among those who profited from land deals connected to Suah — allegations that have not been verified through any independent judicial process.

Suah rejected the claims outright. Rather than answering through legal channels, he branded Gbeisay a “security enemy” and publicly urged President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to remove him from the bench. He also challenged whether Gbeisay had genuine ties to Nimba County or any standing to weigh in on its land affairs.

Adding another layer to the controversy, former Superintendent Cooper testified during proceedings before Gbeisay that he and others had already returned a separate parcel of land in Ganta to Suah in an earlier attempt to settle overlapping claims — though it remains unclear whether that parcel has any bearing on the property at the center of the recent evictions.

With the fresh summons, Suah’s public comments about the Chief Justice may now themselves become the subject of judicial proceedings, adding a new legal front to a dispute that has already spanned the courts, the community, and the media.

Gbeisay continues to frame the matter as simple enforcement of a lawful court order, distancing the Supreme Court from direct blame. Suah and affected residents, meanwhile, argue the real issue is how long-term occupants were treated and whether the eviction process was fair. Neither man has been found to have committed wrongdoing by any judicial body, and both sets of allegations remain unproven.

A motion challenging the underlying judgment is reportedly set for a December hearing, leaving the core ownership dispute — and the increasingly personal battle between a sitting Chief Justice and a former mayor — unresolved for now.

World.title: Kangwa suspension cost Zambia – Musonda
World.content:
Zambia legend Charles Musonda says Chipolopolo paid heavily for Kings Kangwa’s absence in the 3-1 defeat to Algeria in the opening 2027 AFCON qualifier.

Kangwa, now with Greek giants Panathinaikos, missed Friday’s clash at the Hocine Aït Ahmed Stadium after being slapped with a CAF suspension for accumulating two yellow cards in Zambia’s final group game at the last AFCON in Morocco.

Zambia launched Group I with a loss, conceding twice after Fashion Sakala’s 57th minute equaliser had cancelled Jaouen Hadjam’s second-minute opener.

For ex-midfield dynamo Musonda, the aggressive line-up fielded by coach George Lwandamina – four players capable of scoring – lacked balance without Kangwa’s influence.

“For the first time in a long time, I saw a team with four players capable of scoring. We definitely missed the boy from Greece in midfield,” Musonda said.

Musonda also offered a blunt translation of Lwandamina’s post-match comment that Algeria “can make 10 teams” because of their population.

“When Chicken George says ‘population’ he means talent. Today, I am seeing Zambian players performing. That is how a national team should be selected on merit. Club level performance matters,” he said.

The former Anderlecht and Mighty Mufulira Wanderers icon weighed in on the goalkeeping debate after Willard Mwanza shipped three in Tizi Ouzou.

“Decide who your No. 1 goalkeeper is and trust him. Even the best make mistakes. Confidence matters. Mweene knows better. You can’t question him,” he said, backing trainer Kennedy Mweene.

Musonda praised captain Sakala for earning his place with a brilliant goal and constant threat, but demanded more defensive discipline.

“Nobody is bigger than the team. If you want your place, earn it through performances. Sakala did exactly that, brilliant goal and always looked dangerous but should help to make the defensive block even ‘K’ right side must do it,” he said.

He insisted Zambia has enough firepower to recover, listing Patson Daka “Cagliari boy”, Edward Chilufya “Sobolo”, Lameck Banda and the Tanzania-based contingent, but warned against individualism.

“We have options.. Daka, Sobolo, Lameck Banda and the Tanzanian boy. The talent is there. But they should not be selfish in front of goal. It’s the team that scores not an individual.”

Musonda, 1988 African Footballer of the Year runner-up, said he watched Togo’s 1-0 win over Burundi in Lomé, which left Zambia bottom of Group I, but believes Algeria-Zambia was the more competitive tie.

“I watched Togo-Burundi. Algeria-Zambia was more competitive but don’t take any team lightly. Football isn’t played on paper.. it’s played on the pitch. 90 plus minutes.”

With Chipolopolo now needing to beat Togo on September 29 at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola to keep their qualification hopes alive, Musonda called for unity.

“Now let’s stop talking and support the team in Ndola. We are a footballing nation from way back when our population was even less but had talent,” he said.

World.title: Government committed to promote peace, development
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has assured the international community that Zambia remains committed to peace, democracy and inclusive development, following the country’s recently concluded general elections.

President Hichilema has noted that Zambians exercised their constitutional right to choose their leaders during the polls, in line with Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights which affirms that the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government.

He has stressed that Zambia is not at war, but remains peaceful, stable and sovereign, noting that the democratic process should never be mistaken for conflict or instability.

The Head of State said this in a General Debate Statement delivered for him by Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe, during the United Nations General Assembly, in New York.

President Hichilema said despite political differences that naturally accompany elections, Zambia has demonstrated that such differences can and must be managed peacefully through constitutional and legal institutions.

President Hichilema reaffirmed the government’s unwavering commitment to preserving Zambia’s long-standing tradition of peace, stressing that authorities would continue to ensure political differences are addressed through due process of the law.

He added that the calm atmosphere before, during and after the elections reflects the Zambians’ enduring commitment to peace, democracy, national unity and constitutional governance.

The Head of State however added that measures would be taken, within the confines of the Constitution, to prevent disputes from degenerating into violence, armed mobilisation, and insurgency or militia groups.

He further encouraged partners to view Zambia through the lens of peace and stability, and to deepen support for programmes that promote inclusive economic growth, job creation, infrastructure development, human capital development, agriculture, energy, health and other priority areas.

“Our message is clear: Zambia is at peace, Zambia is open for partnership, and Zambia is ready to grow,’’ the Head of State emphasised.

He further expressed appreciation to international election observation missions for what he described as their invaluable support and contribution to Zambia’s democratic process.

The General Debates Session was held under the theme, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All,’’ he stated.

World.title: Veep calls on Chiefs to promote peace, unity
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango has appealed to traditional leaders to continue promoting peace and unity in the country as a pre-requisites for national development.

Mrs Nalumango underscored the need for stability if developmental initiatives such as the Grow Zambia Agenda are to be successful.

Mrs Nalumango said this in a speech read for her by Minister of Green Economy and Environment, Gilbert Siame during the Walamo traditional ceremony of the Lungu people of Mpulungu district.

The Vice President highlighted the significant role traditional leadership plays in ensuring national building, and in the preservation of culture, and tradition.

“Let us build a country where culture and development walk hand in hand, a country where a child will be in school in the morning, and dance at the Walamo ceremony in the evening with pride and dignity,” Mrs Nalumango said.

And Mrs Nalumango says the government recognises the rich mineral endowments in Mpulungu and that the government will endeavor to ensure the full exploitation of minerals for the benefit of local people.

The Vice President added that Mpulungu district is well-positioned to contribute to renewable energy.

“I have been informed that there is potential for high grade lithium in this area and we all know that it is important for clean energy,” she said.

She further emphasised the need for responsible mining activities and ensuring that water sources remain safe.

Mrs Nalumango also called on young people to take advantage of the small-scale and artisanal fund under the Ministry of Mines and Mineral Development once operational and benefit from it.

And Senior Chief Tafuna, Mwine bu Lungu, Chimwando II, reiterated his chiefdom’s commitment to fostering national healing in the post-election period.

Speaking through his representative, Jane Sakala, Senior Chief Tafuna said people of bu Lungu will continue to preach peace and tolerance.

“Elections come and go, but our country remains, let us not allow politics to divide us,” he said.

The 2026 Walamo Traditional Ceremony was celebrated under the theme “Preserving our cultural, traditional, and customary heritage.

World.title: FAZ appoints Copper Queens Assistant Coaches
World.content:
The Football Association of Zambia (FAZ) has appointed ZESCO Ndola Girls Head Coach, Florence Mwila and Technical Advisor Wisdom Zulu as first and second assistant coaches on an interim basis to reinforce the Copper Queens technical bench ahead of the back-to-back 2028 Olympic qualifiers against Uganda.

The appointments are with immediate effect.

FAZ General Secretary, Charles Chakatazya disclosed this in a press statement released to ZANIS in Lusaka today.

Chakatazya said the two coaches have been called by the FAZ Technical Committee to assist Head Coach, Charles Haalubono prepare the Copper Queens for the two-legged Olympic qualifier against Uganda.

ZESCO Ndola Girls Head Coach, Florence Mwila, who is also Head Coach of the Zambia Under-20 Women’s National Team, guided the Copper Queens to victory at the 2024 COSAFA Women’s Championship as interim coach.

She became the first female coach to lead Zambia to the regional title and previously served as Assistant Coach to the late Copper Queens Coach, Bruce Mwape.

The Copper Queens will face Uganda in an away match in Kampala on October 8, 2026 in their first leg of the 2028 Olympic qualifier, while the return game will be played home at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium on October 13, 2026.

Chakatazya said FAZ will continue supporting the technical bench as the Copper Queens seek to qualify for their third consecutive Olympic Games.

The FAZ General Secretary has also called on soccer fans and all football stakeholders to rally behind the ‘girls’ including an all-local technical bench.

World.title: Government making strides to build local vaccine manufacturing
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says Zambia is making deliberate efforts to build capacity for local vaccine manufacturing as part of measures to strengthen the country’s health security and resilience against future epidemics.

President Hichilema has noted that Zambia has increased investment in the health sector, aimed at building a stronger, more resilient system capable of safeguarding lives and livelihoods, while positioning the country to contribute meaningfully to global health security.

He has, however, noted that despite these gains, Zambia remains vulnerable to epidemics therefore calling for the expedited conclusion of negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex under the WHO Pandemic Agreement.

The Head of State said this in a General Debate Statement delivered for him by Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe, during the United Nations General Assembly, in New York.

The President reported that the government increased domestic budgetary allocations to the health sector from approximately 7 percent to over 10 percent, enabling the recruitment of health workers, expansion and modernisation of health infrastructure, and improved availability of essential medical supplies.

He however stressed the importance of strengthened access to technology and enhanced preparedness capacities to detect and respond to future health threats.

President Hichilema further urged the international community to build a fairer global system that provides developing countries with affordable financing, policy space for economic transformation, and stronger climate action backed by adequate resources.

He said Zambia continues to face the devastating effects of droughts, floods and changing weather patterns, which have severely impacted agriculture, food security, water availability, energy generation and livelihoods.

The Head of State stressed that while climate impacts transcend borders, vulnerable nations such as Zambia should not be left to bear the greatest costs despite contributing least to global emissions.

He called for predictable, accessible and affordable climate finance, technology transfer, and greater investment in adaptation and resilience, consistent with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.

“For Africa, adaptation is not optional. Our farmers require climate-resilient agriculture; our communities and cities need resilient infrastructure; our energy systems must become more diversified; and our water resources, forests and ecosystems must be protected,” the President stressed.

President Hichilema also reaffirmed Zambia’s commitment to strengthening water security, climate resilience and sustainable management of natural resources, while ensuring that climate and water action delivers tangible benefits for future generations.

He noted Zambia’s active participation in preparations for the 2026 United Nations Water Conference, where the country is co-chairing the Interactive Dialogue on Water for Cooperation with Finland, emphasising the importance of water security to climate resilience and sustainable development.

World.title: Government committed to supporting traditional ceremonies
World.content:
Lusaka Province Permanent Secretary Joe Kalusa has reaffirmed Government’s commitment in supporting traditional Ceremonies across the country.

Mr Kalusa emphasised that traditional Ceremonies play a critical role in fostering national development.

He was speaking when he officiated at the Dantho traditional ceremony of the Chikunda people of Luangwa district in Chief Mphuka’s Chiefdom.

Permanent Secretary also disclosed that the Government has recorded success in sensitising farmers on innovative farming techniques and practical demonstrations through the department of agriculture.

He said the Government continues to support Agriculture in order to uplift the living standards of the people.

Mr Kalusa also disclosed that 240 farmers in Chief Mphuka’s Chiefdom benefited from the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

“Farmers have already received inputs in time and we are hopeful that this 2026/2027 will be a successful farming season,” said Mr Kalusa.

Chief Mphuka, who was represented by Datho Organising Committee Secretary, Ziphani Phiri, said the traditional ceremony is important in remembering the ancestors and promoting peace among the Chikunda people.

“This traditional ceremony is performed in a small hut which contains twelve clay pots bearing the names of our ancestors, where prayers are offered asking them to provide enough rainfall and a season free from drought,” he explained.

Chief Mphuka also expressed gratitude to the Government for the early distribution of farming inputs to the farmers in his Chiefdom.

Feira Member of Parliament, Emmanuel Tembo appealed to authorities to ensure that the challenge of Human-Animal conflict should be addressed.

Mr Tembo expressed concern that community members’ crop harvests are usually affected by the elephants in particular, that end up eating the produce in the crop fields.

“Our members’ crops yields are usually low because of animals destroying their crops and I therefore appeal that we find a way to reduce the number of elephants that have since increases in number, making it difficult for our farmers to protect their fields when attacked,” bemoaned Mr Tembo.

The Dantho Traditional Ceremony that was celebrated under the theme “Dantho: Our culture, our unity, and our Future “attracted traditional leaders, government officials and other stakeholders from across the province.

World.title: HCAZ calls on stakeholders to invest, support gastronomy industry
World.content:
Hotel and Catering Association of Zambia (HCAZ) past president, Christopher Nsenje has called on stakeholders in the country to work together and invest in Zambian people, local produce and their potential to promote the growth of the country’s gastronomy industry.

Mr Nsenje says there is need for concerted efforts to build a future where Zambian gastronomy can flourish and benefit current and future generations

He said the gastronomy industry also provides opportunities for small businesses to grow by giving them a platform to showcase their products and services alongside bringing together food, culture, tradition, history, identity and the country’s heritage.

He was speaking in Lusaka last evening during the second edition of the Zambia Gastronomy Awards.

Mr Nsenje also presented certificates to winners in various categories during the awards ceremony such as best hotel promoting food and culture, best food market, best African restaurant, best African chef, best Zambian traditional song, and best Zambian traditional dance group.

He said the awards provide a platform to showcase and promote the talent and creativity of Zambian chefs, farmers, entrepreneurs, hotels and other players in the food industry.

Mr Nsenje said promoting Zambian cuisine can help strengthen agriculture, create livelihoods, boost tourism and preserve the country’s cultural heritage.

He has since called on the government, the corporate sector and other stakeholders in tourism, agriculture and related sectors to partner with the industry in promoting Zambian gastronomy.

And Tourism Council of Zambia Board member, Chanda Mwale said gastronomy is a key component of the tourism industry as tourists seek to experience the culture and identity of destinations they visit.

Ms Mwale said Zambia’s ambition to achieve five million tourist arrivals requires the country to strengthen its culinary tourism offering.

She said the Tourism Council of Zambia is committed to supporting the development of a culinary value chain that creates jobs, supports local farmers and promotes authentic Zambian cuisine.

She said the Zambia Gastronomy Awards are helping create a platform for chefs, hotels, restaurants and other players in the hospitality industry to showcase their talents and contribute to tourism development.

She congratulated all the nominees and winners and urged stakeholders to work together to position Zambia as a leading culinary tourism destination as the country works towards its five million tourist arrivals target.

Meanwhile, Zambia Gastronomy Awards Founder, Sonika Mbewe called for increased sponsorship and funding to enable the awards to grow and benefit more players in the food industry.

Ms Mbewe said the awards bring together hotels, chefs, food vendors, musicians and other service providers, thereby creating employment opportunities.

World.title: NAPSA urges public to embrace supplementary savings product
World.content:
National Pension Scheme Authority (NAPSA) Chief Executive officer, Muyangwa Muyangwa has called on members of the public to take advantage of a new product introduced by the institution, called Supplementary Savings, to build their wealth and contribute to economic development.

Mr Muyangwa says the product is designed to provide both the informal and formal sectors with another avenue for saving money and securing their future.

Speaking in an interview with the media, he said the product has no limitations on how much an individual can save, adding that people can save any amount at any given time.

‘’NAPSA is for everyone, both the informal and formal sectors, and we want to appeal to every individual to take advantage of this product and grow their wealth,” he said.

Meanwhile, a fourth-year student at the University of Zambia (UNZA), Natasha Mpashi, has urged her fellow students and the youth at large to take advantage of the new product and start saving for the future.

Ms Mpashi said young people can start saving now to prepare for their future endeavors.

She said the savings could help them venture into economic activities and enhance their livelihoods.

Ms Mpashi further said the product provides people in the informal sector, such as marketeers and other traders, an opportunity to save part of the income they generate.

“This product is very attractive because it caters for both the formal and informal sectors,” she said.

World.title: Africa: Africa's Mineral Strength Is Wasted If Countries Don't Work Together - New Report
World.content:
The OCP Group in Morocco, which holds vast reserves of phosphate - a key ingredient in fertilisers, is responsible for the country's extraction, processing, manufacturing, and export of phosphate products.

analysis

Green technologies are mineral-intensive: electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, wind turbines and grids need cobalt, lithium, copper, manganese, graphite and rare earths. The International Energy Agency estimates that electric cars require six times more minerals than a petrol or diesel car. A wind power plant requires about nine times more minerals than a gas-fired plant.

As the global green transition speeds up, the growing demand for green technologies and minerals creates an opening for Africa, which has deposits of several of the minerals needed.



Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Yet just having these minerals in the ground does not automatically create industries or shared prosperity. In fact, developing countries endowed with minerals often struggle to benefit economically from mining.

We are scholars of how countries build industries and reshape their economies. Our latest study, commissioned by the World Bank, explored how far African countries have moved beyond mining the minerals needed for the energy transition. We examined whether they are processing and refining these minerals or making components for green technologies that use them.

Our analysis followed four steps. First, we identified the transition minerals found in each African country. Second, we examined trade data to see which countries export these minerals and where they are sold.



Third, we looked at where African countries participate in the value chain of green technology. We wanted to find out whether they only mine the mineral and then export it raw, or whether they process it before selling it or produce a final product for sale, such as solar panels. Fourth, we reviewed national and regional mineral and industrial policies.

We found that African countries have deposits of 41 minerals that are used across bioenergy, electricity networks and infrastructure, batteries, energy storage and electric vehicles, and carbon capture and storage. These minerals are also sought after for fuel cells and hydrogen, geothermal energy, heat pumps, hydropower, nuclear power, solar power and wind power.

However, most African countries still export transition minerals in raw or lightly processed form rather than turning them into higher-value materials, components and finished products.



African countries therefore have only a very small presence in the green-technology industries that depend on these minerals. As a result, Africa's mineral wealth has not yet led to high levels of industrial activity, well-paid jobs, higher incomes or wide improvements in living standards.

We found that national and regional institutions are taking steps to change this, but most initiatives are still at an early stage.

Collective mineral strength, shallow value capture

Our research found deposits, reserves, or production of at least one transition mineral in 48 African countries. South Africa had 24 of the 41 minerals; Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) each had 14.

Collectively, Africa holds about 96% of global platinum group metal reserves, 77% of phosphate reserves, and 55% of cobalt reserves. Phosphate and cobalt are used in electric vehicle batteries, while platinum is used in technologies that produce and use green hydrogen.

Yet most countries individually accounted for only small global shares. This matters because small national volumes can make it harder for a country acting alone to influence buyers, attract large processing plants, build complete supply chains or compete with established producers elsewhere.



Trade data reinforces these findings. Notably, apart from South Africa, Nigeria and the DRC, most African countries exported less than 1% of each mineral globally. For several minerals, such as nickel, rare earths, silver and lithium, Africa's five largest exporters together supplied less than 10% of world exports.

African countries could strengthen their position in mineral markets by coordinating their trade policies rather than acting separately. Private companies hold mining licences, but permission to extract minerals does not always include an unrestricted right to export them. Governments may therefore have some scope to coordinate trade rules. How this would work alongside companies' existing rights, and whether it would require their agreement, needs to be further studied.



A deeper weakness identified in our study is limited local processing of minerals. This mainly happens in a few countries such as South Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The processing these countries do often involves crushing and concentrating ore, rather than making products from the mineral.

African countries lose out because of this. For example, Congolese cobalt can sell for US$5.80 per kilogram at the point of extraction. But after local refining, the price increases to US$16.20 per kilogram, nearly tripling its value.

A green economy built on old dependencies

Asia (China in particular) is the leading importer of 16 minerals from Africa. It imported over 30% of those exports on average, and was the second biggest buyer of six other green transition minerals.

Our research found that China absorbed over 40% of Africa's annual mineral ore exports. This shows that Africa is repeating a familiar pattern: mining raw materials while other countries turn them into more valuable products.



The history of Africa, plus low industrialisation levels, means that African countries are also almost invisible in green technology value chains. Between 2017 and 2023, Africa's global patent share across the technologies studied remained below 0.4%, while its export share was below 1% in every category. African countries currently participate in the green economy more as consumers, rather than producers.

African governments are asserting agency

We also found that African governments are changing mining laws, restricting exports, taking ownership stakes and forming partnerships to gain more from their minerals. They want more processing, investment, jobs and income to stay at home. Most are acting individually, although some are working together across borders.

Acting alone has limits. Many countries supply too little to influence large international buyers. If one country demands higher prices or local processing, buyers can shop elsewhere.

Many also lack reliable electricity, affordable loans, transport and skilled workers to process minerals and make components.

Close 

What needs to happen next

Africa is very strong in minerals as a continent. However, deeper regional cooperation would help African countries build industries, not simply trade more easily with one another, a central thesis of a related study, Integrating Africa: From Threads to Hubs. Pooling mineral supplies, markets, infrastructure and skills could lower costs and give them more power when negotiating with global companies. A shared processing centre serving countries across Africa would also help the continent.



To make this happen, African finance and mineral institutions and national governments must agree on common priorities and similar rules about how minerals are processed, and how environmental damage is managed.

Development finance has a role to play. Regional development banks and other African financiers could help fund shared electricity, transport and mineral-processing infrastructure, while universities and businesses develop the technical skills these industries need.

Partnerships with foreign governments and companies should also go beyond extracting and exporting minerals. They should include commitments to process more minerals in Africa, share technology and know-how, train workers, and help local firms become suppliers to emerging green industries.

Gideon Ndubuisi, Assistant Professor of Economics, Delft University of Technology

Elvis Korku Avenyo, Associate professor, University of Johannesburg

Solomon Owusu, Assistant Professor of Global Economic Policy, Boston University

Woubet Kassa, Economist, American University

World.title: Sudan: RSF Drones Strike El Gezira Fuel Depot As Both Sides Report Shootdowns
World.content:
Wad Madani — Paramilitary Rapid Support Forces drones struck the Umm Alila fuel depot east of Wad Madani in El Gezira early on Sunday, triggering fires as Sudan's warring sides reported further drone activity across the country.

Residents said they heard several explosions shortly after dawn prayers in Abu Haraz, about 20 kilometres northeast of Wad Madani. Videos circulating online showed flames across parts of the depot as Civil Defence teams worked to contain the blaze.

The facility stores and distributes petrol and diesel across El Gezira. Civil Defence said it contained the fire and prevented it from reaching other tanks, with damage limited to the petrol and diesel tanks.

'Drones shot down'

The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) said on Thursday that its air defences shot down an FH-95 drone northeast of El Kokiti in North Kordofan, the second drone of the same type it said it had downed this week.

North Kordofan has seen an escalation in fighting in recent weeks.

The RSF, meanwhile, said it shot down a Turkish-made Bayraktar drone over the Blue Nile region on Thursday. It accused the army of systematic attacks on populated areas and called on the international community and regional organisations to condemn them.

World.title: Ethiopia: UN Voices Grave Concern As Fighting Spreads Across Northern Ethiopia
World.content:
An ambulance damaged during the conflict in the Tigray region, stands idle outside a health centre in Gijet in July 2021.

The UN said on Friday it remains gravely concerned by the continued deterioration of the security situation across northern Ethiopia, as fighting spreads across multiple fronts and increasingly disrupts humanitarian operations.

Briefing reporters in New York, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the UN was "particularly troubled by reports of the use of drones as well as incidents of harm to civilians," and again urged all parties to "exercise maximum restraint and address their differences through dialogue."

He said Secretary-General António Guterres was following developments closely and continues to engage on the issue with leaders in New York in a bid to de-escalate the growing crisis - which threatens to return the country to the state of full-scale war in the north which erupted in Tigray in 2020.



Internet outages

According to news reports, internet and call services have been largely cut across the Tigray region. Many rely on banking and mobile transactions due to lack of access to cash and bank ATMs.

The 2020-2022 Tigray war began after political tensions between Ethiopia's federal government and the region's former ruling party, the TPLF, erupted into fighting between Government troops and Tigrayan militia in November 2020.

Eritrean forces joined on the Government's side, and the conflict spread into neighbouring regions, with the UN documenting widespread atrocities and warning of famine-like conditions before it ended two years later.

The UN welcomed the peace deal of November 2022 under African Union mediation, though it continued to flag slow progress on implementation as a risk to the peace now under threat from this week's escalation.

UN mediation

The Secretary-General's Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa, Guang Cong, is engaging with national and regional interlocutors and coordinating closely with partners, including the AU and regional intergovernmental body IGAD, to support a resumption of dialogue under 2022 accord, Mr. Dujarric said.

On the humanitarian front, the UN aid coordination office (OCHA) said the escalation risks adding to already substantial needs, including among civilians displaced by previous fighting in Tigray, in an area also experiencing below-average rainfall linked to the El Niño weather pattern - which promises to exacerbate already extreme weather conditions worldwide.

The UN and partners are continuing regular humanitarian operations where security allows, in Tigray as well as the northern regions of Amhara and Afar, assessing emergency needs.

Fighting chokes off aid

Close 

But insecurity is already taking its toll: this past Sunday, a drone strike in northwestern Tigray hit a truck carrying food assistance for internally displaced people.

Road closures have paused or displaced planned humanitarian movements, Mr. Dujarric said, while operations in parts of Amhara face significant constraints, including the seizure of humanitarian vehicles by armed groups.

The UN stressed that all parties must ensure safe and unhindered access for humanitarian partners to reach those in need, wherever they are.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, also issued a strong statement on Friday saying he was deeply alarmed by the escalation and urged all parties to de-escalate tensions and avoid a return to full-scale war.

He said reported airstrikes hit five schools in Tigray on 22 September, and a mortar strike two days later killed civilians in Kobo, Amhara.

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia's Foretold War Arrives
World.content:
analysis

No one can claim that a return to war in Tigray and northern Ethiopia is a surprise, but it makes it no less horrifying. In just a handful of days, and after months of spiralling tensions and sporadic fighting, the 'grey conflict' the federal government pursued against Tigray has escalated into ''full-blown war,' in the words of Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) vice president Ammanuel Assefa.

The atrocities of the Tigray war are all too recent in the mind; the estimated deaths of 600,000 people, massacres at Axum and Adigrat, the incessant drone strikes on schools, hospitals, and industry, the rape and sexual assault of over 120,000 girls and women, and the harrowing consequences of the man-made famine. To be facing a return to a broader conflict not even four short years after the Pretoria agreement was signed is catastrophic, and this time, threatens to intersect with the metastasising Sudanese civil war.

On Sunday, a diverse coalition of Ethiopia's ethnic-based opposition movements announced a new alliance, unveiled by Fano commander Zemane Kassie on Tigrai TV. Among them are the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), and three smaller ethno-nationalist movements from Afar and the Benishangul-Gumuz regions. Operating under the title of the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, these groups are united by their stated intention to oust the federal government led by PM Abiy Ahmed, and little else. The alliance has been a year in the making, emerging out of the Eritrea-TPLF rapprochement known as 'Tsimdo,' with its core appearing to be the TPLF and Fano; the OLA's commitment seems more circumspect. Still, by mid-week, fighting had renewed on a large scale on several fronts in Amhara and Afar, with over two dozen federal airstrikes reported in several locations, whilst the TPLF seized control of three key airports in Tigray.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The fog of war is immense, and with the situation on the ground so fluid, much remains unknown. Both sides are seeking to paint the other as the aggressor, and how this escalates in the volatile theatre of northern Ethiopia-partially bordering Eritrea and Sudan-is of huge concern. So far, though, fighting has reportedly been concentrated along the Tigray-Afar and Tigray-Amhara borders, as well as the Kobo-Tumuga road in North Wollo, with Tigrayan and Fano purportedly fighting side by side for the first time. Including Abala and Erebti in Afar, Tigrayan units have seized several towns, setting up a potential push across the edge of the Danakil's salt and potash belt towards the Djibouti Corridor, through which most of Ethiopia's trade flows. Armed movement toward the ancient town of Lalibela has also been reported, with Ethiopian Airlines cancelling flights there, as well as to Mekelle, Aksum, and Shire.

Significantly, reports of fresh fighting along the Tekeze River near the Eritrean border emerged yesterday as well, accompanying government drone strikes and Eritrean troop advances into Western Tigray, suggesting that Asmara may be throwing its weight behind its Amhara nationalist and TPLF allies. Eritrea's potential role in the coming days and weeks- beyond shaping the Tigrayan, Fano, and Sudanese army ties and facilitating weapons-- will no doubt prove hugely significant. Ironically, Asmara's transformation from pariah state in the Horn to king-maker lies at the door of Abiy and the Gulf states who ushered in the transactional 'peace deal' in 2018 that paved the way for the Tigray war. It is another cruel twist of fate, and Addis's own short-sighted regional strategy, that places Mekelle and Asmara on the same side after Eritrean troops plundered and massacred their way across much of Tigray in the last war. But- as ever- Isaias Afwerki's strategic logic is one of survival, seeking to place any burden of war on Ethiopia and spare his depleted army. Whether Addis has the appetite to strike at the Eritrean supply lines that will furnish this war remains to be seen.

Mekelle and Addis, as well as Asmara, have been on a war footing for months, reshuffling respective units and commanders, sourcing weapons for the looming conflict, and trading barbs on a host of issues, particularly the status of the Pretoria agreement- which ended the fighting but failed to resolve the brutal Tigray war of 2020-2022- and PM Abiy Ahmed's quasi-imperial desire for 'access to the sea.' In February, battle-ready federal forces were redeployed from the raging insurgencies in Oromia and Amhara to the edges of Tigray, then abruptly stood down. Some had hoped that the surging fuel costs from the US-Iran war might have deterred a return to war, with Addis having budgeted for 4.2 million tonnes of fuel this year before the metastasising war across the Middle East sent costs skyrocketing. But the reprieve has lasted just a season.

In August, substantial, multi-day clashes erupted in Western Tigray between federal and Tigrayan forces. Even then, flickers of diplomacy did nothing to avert the impending broader conflict, with global attention still trained on the fallout of American adventurism in the Middle East now spilling over into Yemen. At the same time, government drone strikes ramped up in Tigray, one of Addis's favoured tools, which have been deployed en masse against the Fano and OLA insurgencies in the Amhara and Oromia regions, respectively. As such, the growing conflagration in northern Ethiopia is another indictment of Abiy's militarised, marketplace style of politics. Unable to conquer Tigray in 2020-2022, Addis has wielded the Pretoria agreement to delegitimise Mekelle, disregarding its responsibilities for dialogue to instead stoke division and pressure Tigray. In particular, Western Tigray was never restored to Mekelle's control, nor was the broader region reintegrated into the federal contract, stranding it in a debilitating limbo.

Mekelle has hardly helped itself either. In the past 18 months, the TPLF has steadily asserted increasing political and military control of the region, stifling dissenting voices and introducing forced conscription. In May, it pushed out Tadesse Werede and installed a council headed by Debretsion Gebremichael, who led Tigray through the last war. But the TPLF is not the party it was six years ago, let alone thirty. It is a poor simulacrum of its former self, bitterly divided and inward-looking, unable to muster support from a wearied Tigrayan population. The cohesion that sustained Tigray against the Derg and the 2020-2022 war has dissipated, and tens of thousands of Tigrayans have fled ahead of the renewed conflict in recent months. Reports from Tigray in the past 48 hours further suggest that those suspected of potential disloyalty, including Tadesse Werede, have been detained.

Questions, too, about the broader alliance remain. Though Fano, Eritrea, and Tigray actors have been coordinating for months, the extent of the new alliance is less clear. Kjetil Tronvoll has aptly referred to it as one of "constructive ambiguity", with the parties bound by little more than an antipathy towards the Addis regime. And though the TPLF vice-president Ammanuel Assefa has pledged to "sit at the table later to solve our problems peacefully," the situation today reflects how fractured the Ethiopian body politic is. For instance, whilst the Fano commanders in Gojjam and Wollo may have fewer qualms with this Tigrayan alliance, those closer to the disputed territories in Western Tigray - who actively participated in the ethnic cleansing of the fertile region in late 2020 and 2021 - are likely to baulk. Still, if these arrayed forces can establish a coherent command centre to coordinate operations in several regions, it will no doubt heap further pressure on the federal government.

The international community--or what remains of it--has responded by urging dialogue and cooler heads to prevail. But on Sudan, and now on Ethiopia, the African Union and foreign capitals have repeatedly failed to rein in the belligerents or their foreign backers. Pretoria was a hastily expanded cessation-of-hostilities document, a flawed handful of paragraphs that failed to address the war's root causes. Even so, the African Union abdicated its role as mediator, whilst its observers failed to hold the parties accountable or convene comprehensive talks. This week, a handful of embassies issued condemnatory statements, including the US offering fulsome support for Abiy, but hopes for any serious intervention remain low. Washington- whilst simultaneously seeking to rehabilitate Eritrea on its prime maritime real estate- and Brussels have broadly prioritised renewing their ties with Addis over holding the federal government accountable to Pretoria despite the drumbeat of a widening war.

What is clear is that humanitarian suffering is set to intensify across northern Ethiopia. Last year, Tigrayan scholar Teklehaymanot G. Weldemichel described Tigray as a "death world", a region deliberately kept in awful precarity. Though Tigray today is not encircled as it was in 2020, a drone strike on a truck ferrying 41 tonnes of food aid bound for the displaced in Sheraro on 20 September recalled the logic of the last war, when famine was induced through the deliberate destruction of the means of survival. Cash is already running short, and with the rains failing and the campaigning season beginning, the lean months will fall inside the war. The humanitarian situation in much of the Amhara region - with the countryside dominated by Fano and urban centres by government forces - is equally dire.

2026 is not 2020, and this cascading Ethiopian conflict comes with Sudan, and the Red Sea, aflame. For the past two years, fears of a renewed Tigrayan-Ethiopian-Eritrean conflict have centred on its convergence with broader Horn instability, with Sudan's internationalised civil war and competing Gulf and Middle Eastern powers backing its protagonists, increasingly connecting conflicts once treated as separate. Since late 2025, Ethiopia has moved more squarely into supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), with whom it shares an Emirati paymaster, hosting an Emirati-facilitated camp for the paramilitaries at Mengi near the Sudanese border. At the same time, another ally of the Sudanese army, Egypt, has aggressively pursued Ethiopia's encirclement over disputes over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) and the Nile water basin, forging closer ties with Eritrea and, to a lesser extent, Somalia and Djibouti.

Close 

Though this conflict is intimately shaped by distinctly Ethiopian grievances, it may quickly assume the intractable characteristics that have dominated the Sudan war --and the tools of the 21st century. External patrons would further complicate the battlefield, making a negotiated settlement harder to reach and military escalation easier to sustain. With the UAE and Saudi Arabia squaring off across the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, yet another conflict offers space for regional competition to seep further into Ethiopia's war. Still, it is early days, and if and how the Sudan war might intersect with the unfolding situation in Ethiopia remains to be seen, but the prospect of a conflict system stretching from Chad to the Djiboutian border makes one shudder.

If this descends into a broader conflict--and the augurs are bleak--it will not follow the script of 2020. Then, the war was broadly contained within Ethiopia's borders. Today, several wars are already running at once, with a host of patrons, no single mediator able to end them and the margins between Ethiopia's conflict and others wafer-thin. And so, in the face of the horrors of 2020-2022 and neighbouring Sudan, Ethiopia has returned to war.

Matthew de Waal is a freelance analyst on peace and security focused on the Horn of Africa and Red Sea based in Nairobi. Until recently, he was the Deputy Head of Research and Publications at Sahan Research, a think-tank focused on conflict and governance in the region. Matthew has a particular focus on the geopolitics of the Horn and Al-Shabaab.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 25, 2026
World.content:
press review

Uganda Begins $121M South Sudan Power Interconnection Project

Uganda has commenced implementation of the South Sudan-Uganda Power Interconnection Project (SUPIP) after securing US$121 million from the African Development Fund (ADF) to finance the Ugandan component of the regional electricity initiative. Combined with counterpart funding from the Ugandan government, the financing will support the construction of high-voltage transmission infrastructure linking Uganda's electricity grid to South Sudan. The project is expected to facilitate cross-border electricity trade, strengthen Uganda's northern transmission network, and provide South Sudan with access to more reliable and affordable power.

Malawi's Electoral Body Under Fire Over Relocation to Blantyre

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Malawi Electoral Commission (MEC) is facing pressure over plans to relocate to Blantyre - the country's commercial capital - alongside a string of staff union grievances that risk undermining public confidence in the body ahead of upcoming elections. An executive order directed MEC to move its headquarters back to Blantyre after it had relocated to Lilongwe in June 2023 to be closer to the seat of government. The commission's staff union has demanded an urgent meeting with leadership, citing unresolved issues surrounding the relocation and lease uncertainties.

Liberian Govt Says Cybercrime Law Doesn't Target Free Speech

Senator Francis Dopoh has reassured Liberians - particularly journalists, activists, and social media users - that the newly enacted cybercrime law is not intended to suppress criticism or peaceful dissent. This clarification follows the recent arrest of an individual over a social media post, which sparked public debate about the legislation. Dopoh said the law instead targets behaviors posing direct threats to individuals, institutions, and national security. He added that its protections for women, girls, and children will help combat online threats, blackmail, and the non-consensual sharing of private images.

Zimbabwe Parliament Wants State of Emergency Over Harare Sewage Crisis

Harare is facing a public health crisis as raw sewage continues flowing into rivers feeding Lake Chivero, the capital's main water source, according to a parliamentary committee report. The report paints a grim picture of Zimbabwe's deteriorating wastewater management system, stating that only 20 of the country's 63 sewage treatment plants are currently operational. Active plants discharge an estimated 570 megaliters of raw sewage daily, worsening pollution levels across major water sources.

The pope prayed at the Grotto Saturday night before leading an open-air Mass on the Prairie on Sunday, with hundreds of thousands expected to be in attendance.

POPE LEO DRAWS STAGGERING 800,000 FAITHFUL TO HEART OF PARIS FOR MASSIVE OUTDOOR MASS

He discussed his upcoming meeting with the pope, who he said was visiting Lourdes in the name of purification and healing, including healing from the Church's recent sexual abuse scandals.

JUST 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER COULD HAVE SURPRISING HEALTH BENEFITS, STUDY FINDS

We all love him!"

Dr. de Franciscis said the pope would meet with people whose miracle healings were investigated and later recognized by the Church.

Those include Sister Bernadette Moriau, who was cured of a spinal condition and was able to walk again, and Antonietta Raco, who in 2009 was cured of the severe neurodegenerative disease primary lateral sclerosis.

MELINDA FRENCH GATES STUNS FESTIVAL CROWD, PLEDGES TO MATCH OLIVIA RODRIGO'S FUNDRAISING FOR $20M HAUL

Following the stunning water display, Rodrigo changed into a tank top and jeans for an encore performance including a few hits from her previous catalogs, "GUTS" and "SOUR."

ED SHEERAN APOLOGIZES FOR MACKLEMORE BACKLASH, ENCOURAGES UNITY AT FIRST CONCERT SINCE FALLOUT

World.title: Supersonic Russian jets trigger joint scramble by NATO allies amid Putin 'clowns' jab
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Finnish and Swedish fighter jets scrambled for the first time on Sept. 24 to intercept supersonic Russian military aircraft flying over the Gulf of Finland, marking a major milestone in Nordic defense cooperation amid heightened tensions with Moscow.

The mission also came one day before Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed European warnings about the threat from Moscow in the region and mocked Estonia's new defense minister over the Baltic state's preparations for a potential Russian attack.

Finnish F/A-18 Hornets and Swedish JAS 39 Gripens were scrambled after Russian aircraft were detected in the international airspace, according to the Swedish Armed Forces.

US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS

The Russian formation included a Tu-134 transport plane, a high-altitude, supersonic MiG-31 interceptors designed to detect and engage long-range threats; and Su-30 multirole fighter jets which are designed for air-to-air and air-to-ground combat.

"This is what close cooperation looks like in practice," Maj. Gen. Jonas Wikman, commander of the Swedish Air Force, said in a statement following the joint operation.

"Built over years on trust and strong personal relationships, we can now operate seamlessly together — as air forces, as nations and as Allies."

Concern over Russian military activity along NATO’s eastern flank has grown following a string of airspace violations.

These include Russian drones entering Polish airspace, a Mi-8 helicopter crossing from Kaliningrad into Poland, drones crashing in Romania and Moldova, and armed Russian jets entering Estonian airspace before being intercepted by NATO aircraft on Sept. 18.

BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT

In Estonia, Defense Minister Martin Herem warned that Russia could be capable of using military force against Estonia within a year and argued that Tallinn must determine whether its defenses are sufficient for such a scenario.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal stated that the government is ready to shut down border crossing points on short notice if threat assessments change, according to reports.

Speaking at the St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum on Friday, Putin pushed back against such warnings.

"Many people in Europe say they expect an attack from Russia and therefore claim they must prepare for war with Russia," Putin said.

"I want to emphasize once again: we are not preparing for military action against Europe. We have no such plans, no basis for them, and, most importantly, no real motive to escalate the situation with Europe."

Putin then mocked Herem's warnings: "As we jokingly say in Russia: 'The circus has left, but the clowns remain.' It is political clowning. ... Clearly, these statements are complete nonsense and absurdity," Putin said, according to EurAsia Daily.

FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE

Estonia sits across the Gulf of Finland from Finland, with the three countries forming part of NATO's increasingly integrated northern and eastern defenses amid concerns about Russian military activity.

Finland formally joined NATO as its 31st member in April 2023, roughly doubling the alliance's land border with Russia. Sweden followed as the 32nd member in March 2024. Estonia, which regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, has been a NATO member since 2004.

The Baltic Sea region has also remained on heightened alert following incidents involving gas pipelines, sabotage and hybrid threats since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Reuters has reported.

NATO said in June that it was enhancing protection of its eastern members in the cyber and space domains while helping countries build resilience against what it describes as hostile Russian actions, including cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace violations.

NATO says its military activities along the eastern flank are entirely defensive and that it is "ready, willing and able to defend every Ally."

FINLAND'S STUBB CREDITS TRUMP FOR PUSHING UKRAINE PEACE TALKS WHILE DISMISSING RUSSIAN INVASION FEARS

The alliance has said an attack against any member would be met with a "resounding response."

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte recently underscored Washington's role in the alliance during a visit to Iowa, telling The Associated Press that Putin "knows that the United States and Europe are totally intertwined."

"We have to make sure that we are prepared, we are strong, and he knows it," Rutte said.

"And if he does anything silly, he knows our reaction will be tough," he warned.

European intelligence officials said Sept. 24 that Russia could test NATO's defenses.

Denmark's Defense Intelligence Service assessed the risk of a limited Russian military attack against a NATO country in the coming months as "low but growing" and said Moscow is expected to intensify its hybrid campaign against NATO and the West.

The service said in a statement that a full-scale Russian invasion of a NATO member remains highly unlikely but can no longer be ruled out.
