World.title: Revisiting zombie towns: Balclutha's rural resilience
World.content:
A decade ago, Shamubeel Eaqub was pessimistic about the future of heartland New Zealand. All the financial indicators were depressing. But something is changing in small regional towns - something surprising.

The controversial economist heads to Balclutha and Tokoroa, where he discovers two communities showcasing rural resilience in different ways.

Who were the winners and losers from economic reforms 40 years ago? How have zombie towns become survivor towns?

Shamubeel Eaqub offers his unique insights into how struggling communities can get their mojo back.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6403979469112

A decade ago I called Whanganui a zombie town. It was slowly losing people, jobs and prospects, and seemingly no one was doing anything about it. Then it went from exporting people to importing them. What did I miss?

I went back to provincial New Zealand to find out. I also wanted to find an antidote to the polarisation that is wrecking our communities and politics.

The term infuriated many. Steve Hill, chief executive of the Clutha District Council, remembers it well. "We were pissed off, right? And it was a challenge to us: how could we prove that term wrong."

He does smile wryly when he says this. In person, people are less outraged and keener to explain why their town is special, why there are things people are trying, and that some things are working.

Audio player for " Zombie Towns: Everything I Missed " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/country/1619719%2Frevisiting-zombie-towns-balclutha-s-rural-resilience

Zombie Towns: Everything I Missed The Detail Download MP3 20m

In my defence, I hadn't named Balclutha. I was describing megatrends that were hollowing out economic opportunities in many places: globalisation, urbanisation, technological change, ageing and climate change. People, especially the young, were voting with their feet.

I was frustrated by a lack of action. Central government had no regional lens. And locally I saw little co-ordinated action to avert the hollowing out, despite businesses, homes and infrastructure that should have meant real opportunities to be harnessed.

The megatrends are still there and intensifying. Whanganui has grown, but not every town has.

So I looked at two places. Tokoroa in South Waikato is living through forestry mill closures now. Balclutha in South Otago has regained its mojo and grown for the past decade, after three decades of hollowing out.

RNZ / Amrita Marks / Supplied

I can see it in the data. In the 1970s Tokoroa was rich, with average incomes 40 per cent above the national average. Today they are 15 per cent below. Balclutha grew in the 1970s, hollowed out from the mid-1980s, and turned about a decade ago.

But I had the data already. This project was about the human stories. There is a connection to place that is not easily captured in economics.

People have roots, connections and hope. It was surprisingly easy to collect the stories. People wanted to be seen, heard and acknowledged.

While I was filming in Balclutha, Nigel Stirling, an ex-RNZ economics correspondent who interviewed me many times, pulled up in his ute. He is back on the family farm.

"This is not a zombie town now," he told me. He is right.

He reckons it's dairy prices and Auckland house prices. Is that true? And what lessons for other places? I found it was much more than Nigel suggested, and the magic sauce is messy, complicated and local.

Economic fallout from Rogernomics was "brutal and fast", according to Bryan Cadogan. RNZ / Supplied

Bryan Cadogan, mayor of Clutha for 15 years until last year, tells me how the district was gutted by Rogernomics 40 years ago, economically and socially. "It was brutal, and it happened fast." Family farms went.

The kids had a saying: Clutha sucks, I'm out of here. They don't say it anymore. What changed, in Bryan's telling, was that the district looked at what it already had.

"We had extremely low section prices, low house prices, and being rural we had an enormous number of jobs. Fifteen years ago there were about a thousand jobs in the Clutha District that weren't filled."

His motto is easy: get a job, get a house, get a life.

The documentary is four video episodes and a seven-part podcast, funded by NZ On Air for Newsroom and RNZ. The next three essays follow Bryan's three themes: a job, a house, a life.

In Tokoroa I met Thelma Popata, who runs the Muscle and Curves gym. "I don't want to leave this place. People pull together to help one another. It's pretty special here." There is a love of and pride for place - a genuine foundation to build from.

World.title: Ministry delays rules on too-hot homes
World.content:
Audio player for " No fix for overheated homes until 2031 " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/community/1619940%2Fministry-delays-rules-on-too-hot-homes

No fix for overheated homes until 2031 Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Advocates for people living in overheating new builds are dismayed that officials will not consider comprehensive changes to fix the issue until 2031.

Residents of the glut of townhouses and apartments built in the last few years have repeatedly raised concerns about dangerous heat in their homes during summer, because of common design flaws.

The Building Research Association (BRANZ) and Green Building Council are among organisations advocating for changes to the Building Code, which currently does not include any controls on overheating or maximum internal temperatures.

However, Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment officials have confirmed they are working on the issue, but it would not be part of a regular code review in 2028, and instead would be considered during the subsequent review in 2031.

"We're really shocked to hear that we're facing a significant delay in dealing with this," Green Building Council chief executive Andrew Eagles said.

"That's hugely alarming when you talk to these families and they're in sweltering conditions."

Green Building Council chief executive Andrew Eagles is among those advocating for urgent regulation changes. Supplied / NZGBC

Jared Laidlaw and his family moved into their two-storey Auckland townhouse at the end of 2021 and discovered almost immediately that the upstairs overheated.

The house was west-facing, with a floor-to-ceiling window in the master bedroom, minimal ventilation, no eaves and no external window shading.

"You just have five or six hours straight of sun smashing that side of the house," he said.

Audio player for " Andrew Eagles discusses concern over overheated homes " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/community/1619940%2Fministry-delays-rules-on-too-hot-homes

Andrew Eagles discusses concern over overheated homes Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Temperatures upstairs typically got to 35°C during the day and were still in the high 20s late in the evening, he said.

Some parts of the house were not just uncomfortable but dangerous - like the aluminium front door, which reached 60° or 70° degrees on a summer day and radiated heat back into the house.

"You can't touch the door - it burns your hand."

When his young sons were born, he and his wife were hyper-vigilant about monitoring the temperature.

"We used to have thermometers and stuff because ... it's not safe for babies."

In the time they had lived in the house, they had tried ceiling fans and a noisy portable air-conditioning unit, and finally paid $2500 for ducted air-conditioning.

He and his next-door neighbour ordered a roll of foil-covered bubble wrap from Temu, which they used to make huge shades that could be attached by Velcro to the internal window frames.

"That has made the biggest difference, aside from the AC," he said.

"This will stay up weeks or months at a time ... We can't enjoy the view because it's 35°C in here during the day."

The features that contributed to overheating at Laidlaw's house were typical of many new-build townhouses and apartments, Andrew Eagles said.

"You've often got windows going floor to ceiling ... you've got no eaves and no shading allowance," he said.

"You're then getting the full effect of the sun during the day and smaller rooms, so the combination of all of that is you just get this massive heat build-up."

File photo Sharon Brettkelly

His organisation and BRANZ both supported an interim fix to a schedule in the Building Code that would require modelling at the design stage to check if a dwelling would overheat.

The software capable of doing that modelling was already used by hundreds of firms around the country, he said.

"I [would] need to put into a calculator the size of the home, the orientation, the size of the windows, and then it comes back and says, oh look - you are going to overheat this proportion of that time."

The design would then have to be tweaked until it was under the modelling limits, Eagles said.

"The steps people are likely going to take is reduce the amount of glazing - that will save them money - or put some shading on or put some eaves on or slightly change the orientation, those sorts of things."

BRANZ senior building physicist Stephen McNeil said without regulation, people in Laidlaw's predicament would suffer even more as average temperatures increased.

"It's also those extremes ... and we have other concerns with the increasing humidity in the air as well."

BRANZ senior building physicist Stephen McNeil. Supplied/Rob Suisted

In a written response, MBIE manager for building performance and engineering Dave Gittings said officials were working through how overheating requirements could be integrated into the Building Code, but overheating was a complex issue without a single fix.

"We need to make sure any changes work together as a package and don't create unintended consequences elsewhere in the building system. That includes considering an approach where designers would need to demonstrate through modelling that their designs will not exceed a maximum indoor temperature."

The 2031 review was appropriate timing because of the considerable technical and policy work involved, he said.

"Overheating is influenced by a broad range of interconnected factors, including solar gain, shading, the heat absorption of building materials, ventilation, airtightness and building orientation. It takes time to consider any consequences, develop options for change and thoroughly consult on any changes to ensure we've considered every angle before implementing them."

The ministry would provide informal guidance to designers and homeowners in the meantime.

Officials were currently looking at how building designs may need to demonstrate they do not exceed maximum indoor temperatures.

Introducing a requirement such as the one proposed by the Green Building Council would involve "more than simply setting a temperature limit", Gittings said.

There would also need to be appropriate capability among those doing the modelling, which would require industry acceptance with any changes, along with clear expectations for building consent authorities about the evidence they should receive, what they needed to check and when specialist review may be required.

But Stephen McNeil said changes could be staged.

"Rather than one big hit where you deliver this perfect regulatory thing that solves every problem, you've got to take the industry on a journey and give them time to build into it," he said.

"Simple measures now will save us a lot of pain down the track because we could capture the riskiest buildings quite early in the piece."

Andrew Eagles said in this case, "perfect is the enemy of good".

"We should just get the bloody hell on with it.

"We've already got people writing to us horrified that they're spending tens of thousands of dollars and that their kids are in rooms that are far, far too hot."

Jared Laidlaw agreed five years was too long to wait.

"I'd anticipate a lot of houses in between now and then are going to be townhouses, so you're going to only exacerbate the situation," he said.

World.title: Here's why it feels like your money is tighter
World.content:
Audio player for " Why do I pay tax on my KiwiSaver? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/personal-finance/1626010%2Fhere-s-why-it-feels-like-your-money-is-tighter

Westpac economists say the price of many things New Zealand households buy every day has risen faster than general inflation over the past 10 years, including butter, bread, mince, and even mince pies and chocolate.

Inflation as measured by the consumer price index (CPI) is up 38 percent since 2016.

But Westpac said some of the things you probably put in your trolley every week have risen much faster.

Milk

The average price for two litres of milk was up 57 percent over 10 years, from an average $3.27 in 2016 to $5.12 this year. In the middle of this year, Stats NZ called out milk as one of the items that was helping to push up food price inflation.

At the time, ASB senior economist Mark Smith said retail milk prices in New Zealand had a six- to nine-month lag from global market movements.

Breakfast biscuits - like Weetbix

Even a basic breakfast of Weetbix hasn't been able to escape the price rise. The average price of a 1.2kg pack of breakfast biscuits was up 27 percent from $6.73 to $8.58, Westpac said.

Olive oil

Olive oil has been one of the big price movers of recent years. Westpac said it was up 40 percent over 10 years, from $12.14 to $17.04. The increase has been blamed on weather and poor harvests.

Butter

Butter prices lifted 157 percent, from $3.28 for a 500g block in 2016 to $8.43, on average. Much of that increase has been in recent years, pushed up by global dairy prices.

Cheese

For similar reasons, cheese has increased in price, too. Westpac said a kilogram of mild cheese became 75 percent more expensive, from $7.39 in 2016 to $12.95 in 2026.

White bread

A loaf of white bread increased in price by 120 percent over the decade. Global wheat prices have been part of the problem.

Canned tomatoes

A can of tomatoes increased in price by 43 percent, from $1.12 in 2016 to $1.60 this year. Fresh tomatoes were up 30 percent. Crop failures have affected tomato prices, as well as rising costs for things like transport.

Beef mince

A kilogram of beef mince increased in price by 71 percent over 10 years, from $14.24 in 2016 to $24.41 now. A much smaller US cattle herd has been credited with pushing up prices around the world, including in New Zealand because we export mot of our beef.

Takeaway coffee

The average price of a takeaway coffee has lifted 41 percent over 10 years, from $3.72 in 2016 to $5.24 this year. Coffee bean prices have increased quickly and many other input costs for cafes have also risen, such as milk, labour and rent.

Other costs

Westpac said the average cost of a GP visit was up 50 percent, a dental exam 41 percent and a tank of 91 fuel for a mid-sized car 66 percent. A warrant of fitness was up 61 percent and a tank of diesel for a mid-sized SUV was up 141 percent.

What hasn't risen so fast?

Westpac NZ managing director of product, sustainability and marketing Sarah Hearn said some items that were more "nice to have" than necessities, such as home furnishing, communications and cultural services such as TV subscriptions had much smaller prices rises.

World.title: Explainer: Can you get arrested for vandalising a campaign sign?
World.content:
Explainer: Election season has officially kicked off, and passions are flying high. But if you get fired up enough to vandalise or destroy a candidate billboard, be warned - the police may end up at your door.

Defacing candidate billboards is a seasonal sport around much of the motu, but police warn that it's still actually a crime, and you may be prosecuted if caught.

Vandalism can range from the somewhat witty, like googly eyes glued on faces, to the nasty, such as racist and sexist comments, to the downright dangerous, such as setting billboards on fire.

RNZ / Nik Dirga

What can you be charged with?

"It is illegal to deface, destroy, or remove election hoardings," a police spokesperson said.

"You can be charged with wilful damage, and if you were to remove one you could be charged with theft."

The penalties for wilful damage can be a prison term of up to three months or a fine of up to $2000, while the penalties for theft depend on the value of the item, but can attract fines or serious prison time.

Arrests aren't just hypothetical.

A man in Tauranga was charged earlier this month after allegedly damaging about 30 hoardings in a two-hour period.

"The damage in some cases is significant and unfortunately that's an unnecessary cost for the people who own them," Senior Sergeant Shannon Clifford said. "We won't tolerate this illegal and destructive behaviour in our community."

Who's getting vandalised?

The vandalism runs across party lines.

The New Zealand Herald reported a National billboard was destroyed in an arson attack in Auckland's Mount Albert recently, requiring a Fire and Emergency callout.

"I have to replace signs that have been damaged when they cut our leader's face out of them," Waikato Labour candidate Jamie Toko wrote on Facebook. "Childish, jealous and threatened. You can't get any smaller than that."

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer shared a photo on social media of one of her signs defaced with a racist slur.

"Our billboards team is made up of my husband, and a few really hearty supporters who work their butts off in between their normal mahi," she wrote.

"We then have beautiful whānau who help to look after, host and now are already having to clean billboards up."

National MP for Hamilton East Ryan Hamilton posted vandalised signs of him and party leader Christopher Luxon on Facebook recently, calling the attackers "cowards."

"If you disagree with me or want to discuss something, pick up the phone, send me an email, or come and have a conversation," he said. "Don't go around under the cloak of darkness vandalising other people's property."

Auckland councillor Josephine Bartley's signs were marked up with abuse during last year's local body elections. LDR / Mary Afemata

The Electoral Commission said they have received some reports about sign vandalism, but encouraged people to contact police.

"The correct place to report theft or vandalism is the police," a spokesperson said.

"Local Councils oversee the rules around where and when signs can go up, so they may also receive complaints or reports."

Of course, vandalism is nothing new.

In past elections, racist attacks have been scrawled on billboards of Chinese candidates and Indian candidates.

Last year during local body elections, Maungakiekie Auckland councillor Josephine Bartley said her signs were marked up with personal abuse, but she couldn't afford to replace them.

"I told the Labour team to leave my billboards. Anything that's vandalised, leave it because I've got a mortgage. I can't afford to keep buying more signs. I'm only buying 30 and that's it."

Hamlton, the National MP, said on Facebook that he would replace his own damaged hoardings.

World.title: Can Labour reclaim a lost heartland in Wellington's newest seat, Wellington Bays
World.content:
Audio player for " Labour targets Greens-held Wellington Bays seat " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1620625%2Fcan-labour-reclaim-a-lost-heartland-in-wellington-s-newest-seat-wellington-bays

Labour targets Greens-held Wellington Bays seat Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Wellington's newest seat is shaping up to be a neck-and-neck race for the left, as Labour tries to reclaim a lost heartland.

Why is it interesting?

Home to more than 66,700 voters, the Wellington Bays electorate encompasses southern and eastern parts of the city and includes three major employers - Wellington Hospital, Wētā Workshop and Wellington Airport.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405111229112

Previously poetically-titled Rongotai - meaning sound of the sea - its boundaries were redrawn last year to capture Mount Cook and Brooklyn, which were both part of the former Wellington Central seat.

As long as it's existed under MMP, the seat has been held by the left.

Labour had it for 24 years, 18 of those with Annette King at the helm, but lost it in 2023 to Green MP Julie Anne Genter.

What happened last election (and what might happen this time)

Genter took the seat by 2717 votes against then Labour rival Fleur Fitzsimmons, with National's Karunā Muthu coming in third.

Speaking to RNZ, King admitted Labour's favourability fell in 2023, dwarfed by a Green momentum that had been building in both seats for several years.

"The tide turned, the votes changed, and so did the seat."

But a recent Taxpayers' Union-Curia* Poll of 400 voters had the party's contender - Council of Trade Unions economist Craig Renney, a former advisor to Grant Robertson - in a deadlock with incumbent Genter at 29 percent for the electorate vote.

Muthu was third on 15 percent.

So who's standing?

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

At 51 on the list, Renney's entry into parliament depends on the electorate fight.

He said the list placement didn't feature in his mind, and he wanted to represent the area.

"Labour's said quite clearly that it doesn't want to deliver the cuts - the indiscriminate cuts - that this government has said it wants to deliver. I want to fight for every public sector job that needs doing."

Genter hoped the voters would give her another stint at pushing for climate solutions and community services.

"Advocate for investment in the infrastructure that's needed to deal with climate change, with the investment in social housing, and the wrap around support services, and of course more frequent, public transport."

Muthu, a Wellington lawyer, is taking another shot.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He wants the second Mount Victoria tunnel to go ahead in a bid to ease congestion to Wellington Airport. It's a multi-billion dollar roading project undergoing fast-track approval, but which has no start-date or funding earmarked for major construction yet.

"We haven't said we are not going to do it...we are going to do it, [the] National Party is the only party that is committed to delivering the second Mount Vic Tunnel."

ACT deputy leader Nicole McKee is also standing as candidate, pointing to stress with recent water bills from Tiaki Wai.

"The concern is the increasing amounts over upcoming years, especially when we have a society, not just Wellington Bays absolutely struggling with the cost of living."

Opportunity's candidate, former WWF New Zealand chief executive Dr Kayla Kingdon-Bebb, said Opportunity was running a party-vote only campaign.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"I think it's fair to say there's no centrist environmental party represented in government right now...we are able to work with the left or the right blocks."

New Zealand First's Gerald Warner is the only candidate not living in the area - he currently resides in Kāpiti.

The public servant said he wants to push for affordable social housing in the suburb, "balanced by responsible management", citing the Arlington and Strathmore Park Kainga Ora developments.

RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

What do the locals say?

Outside the bustling supermarkets in Miramar and Island Bay, many voters RNZ spoke to were still weighing up their options.

"I've always been a bit of swing voter to be honest, I'm old enough to have seen a lot of changes, and a lot of failed policies," resident Alan Rowell said, chuckling.

Dog walker Jess Bennett said improving public transport was her biggest concern.

"[The] buses are so packed in. Kids are sitting on top of the wheel base, falling over, people are having to re-wait again."

At Tandoori Indian Flame restaurant, empty tables were giving manager Rajnish Prasad a headache.

"Many businesses are struggling in Wellington... the last couple of years it's been really really hard," Prasad said, adding that he couldn't hire staff.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

That was a thought echoed by Phil Hughes, at Palmers Garden Centre.

Garden centres had long been considered "recession proof" with people coming in to purchase home-grown vegetables - but that had changed.

He mentioned public sector job cuts, describing that as having a "massive effect" on businesses in the area - with residents either losing jobs, or feeling uncertain about the future.

At the moment, he wasn't sure any of the parties were appealing to him.

"The key thing for me is to give the public somehow some confidence, that they can see that there's a way forward."

"Customers feed off that confidence and hopefully people feel a bit better...but at the moment it's quite challenging."

World.title: Christopher Luxon labels policy by potential coalition partner 'madness'
World.content:
Audio player for " Christopher Luxon discusses National's campaign launch " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1624802%2Fchristopher-luxon-labels-policy-by-potential-coalition-partner-madness

Christopher Luxon discusses National's campaign launch Morning Report Download MP3 8m

National leader Christopher Luxon insists a potential coalition partner's policy is "madness" and will not happen, while lumping the left bloc's "nine new taxes" together as certainties.

National has consistently attacked Labour "and its mates" (the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity) saying combined they would impose nine new taxes.

Labour has only committed to its own capital gains tax.

Meanwhile New Zealand First - National's potential coalition partner - is campaigning on buying back BNZ for around $20 billion.

Christopher Luxon told Morning Report "that's just not going to happen".

"It's absolute madness," he said.

Morning Report's John Campbell put to Luxon that Labour leader Chris Hipkins could say the same for his potential coalition partners' policies.

Luxon said Hipkins would "have to do business" with the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity.

Chris Hipkins at Labour's campaign launch on Sunday. NZME / Supplied

"He can't find a pathway to get into government without those four radical parties and six leaders, that's going to be chaos," he said.

"He is going to implement those nine new taxes."

Both National and Labour held their campaign launches in Auckland on Sunday.

Luxon unveiled a list of 10 promises, including economic growth, no new taxes, better infrastructure and tougher consequences for criminals.

He told the crowd National had delivered this term but "the job isn't done".

Campbell asked Luxon what more he wanted to achieve.

"We've really got to continue to drive really hard into economic growth," he said.

"We can see all the economists talking about our economy strengthening and growing faster than people had anticipated, which is all good, but you know, we want to just continue that plan."

At Labour's launch, Hipkins released a new policy, promising to write off 10 percent of eligible student loan balances.

World.title: National and Labour leaders come out firing - and fed up
World.content:
Audio player for " Jo Moir on National and Labour's campaign launches " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1619352%2Fnational-and-labour-leaders-come-out-firing-and-fed-up

Jo Moir on National and Labour's campaign launches Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Analysis: Both National and Labour's leaders came across as fed-up on Sunday - but for different reasons.

While Christopher Luxon was annoyed by comparisons to his predecessor Sir John Key, Chris Hipkins went full sweary-bear on both National and the media.

The two Chrises were back in Auckland exactly where they started three years ago but wearing the opposite hat - Luxon now juggling the prime minister role with that of National leader, while Hipkins is doing the reverse.

On Sunday the memories of just how bad the 2023 campaign went for Hipkins, who started it as prime minister and finished it with one of the party's worst election results to date, were fresher than perhaps even he realised.

Asked by reporters to reflect on what went wrong last time, he sniped: "Oh you've been listening to the National Party spin bullshit, and I'd encourage you not to".

Chris Hipkins and partner Toni with Labour MPs and candidates at the end of the leader's campaign launch speech at the Due Drop Centre in Manukau, Auckland, on 27 September 2026. Jo Moir / RNZ

Pressed as to why he didn't have any momentum on the last campaign - a campaign he's acknowledged was tough to find a rhythm in - Hipkins fired back angrily: "Yeah we lost and that was quite difficult - we're going to win this one though."

Then in response to why voters hadn't heard about Labour's public transport fare cap policy and whether the party messaging wasn't working, Hipkins countered: "It's probably more of an indictment on all of you people that people aren't listening to you anymore."

During his speech to 600-odd Labour supporters gathered at the Due Drop Centre, he looked and sounded like he was finally firing on all cylinders, ready to hit the ground running.

He called "bullshit" on National's "outright lies" about tax and expressed how "angry" he still is at Luxon over rising prices and the prime minister's response to it.

By the time he fronted reporters he was angry at everyone and everything, with even some of his MPs flanking him looking down at the ground while he unleashed.

Clearly, he's had advice from his team around him that he underperformed three years ago and nobody wants a repeat.

Audio player for " Craig McCulloch reports on Labour’s election campaign launch " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1619352%2Fnational-and-labour-leaders-come-out-firing-and-fed-up

Craig McCulloch reports on Labour’s election campaign launch Morning Report Download MP3 3m

It could be a tough ask, however, for Hipkins to keep up that level of intensity through to the election.

And while an aggressive tone might work in a debate environment when he's going head-to-head with Luxon, he'll need to soften the rhetoric when engaging with voters on the street.

The full show at Labour was a musical spectacle with a powerful Auckland Secondary Schools Pasifika Choir kicking things off, and the crowd stomping their feet and giving multiple standing ovations throughout Hipkins' address.

He harked back to the glory days at one point, announcing a student loan policy that would write-off ten percent of debt for some borrowers, and the whole thing for those who have $2000 or less owing.

Helen Clark, the former Labour leader who won her way into government in 2005 with an interest-free student loan policy, sat near the front of the stage on Sunday as Hipkins unveiled his 2026 version.

It's popular policy and targets key demographics Labour is looking to secure - young people, and those feeling the cost of living crisis the hardest.

National took a different approach, announcing no new policy and instead rolling out for the second campaign launch in a row a pledge card of promises.

As one senior MP told RNZ: "Well if it worked last time, so why do something different."

National leader Christopher Luxon shakes hands as he finishes his party's campaign launch speech on 27 September 2026. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

The pledge card ticked off all the usual National Party stomping grounds of no new taxes, better school results, getting the books in surplus, and better infrastructure.

Where the tried and true fell over for National this year was picking a venue it couldn't fill with party faithful. who were just a little lacklustre in their shows of support.

Many of the lines in campaign chair Simeon Brown and deputy leader Nicola Willis' speeches didn't get the applause they were expecting, and at times pausing for.

While Sir John Key got a hearty dose of rapturous applause, even the cues in Luxon's speech where he bagged Labour and its coalition mates didn't get the cheers he might have expected.

Audio player for " Christopher Luxon discusses National's campaign launch " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1619352%2Fnational-and-labour-leaders-come-out-firing-and-fed-up

Christopher Luxon discusses National's campaign launch Morning Report Download MP3 8m

The glitzy International Convention Centre was set up to seat 1500 but only two-thirds of that arrived - not that Luxon wanted to engage in a question line about it after the launch.

Nor did he take well to being compared to Sir John and his 2011 campaign speech where the Opposition was barely mentioned.

With just 40 days to go until the election neither Chris has time to reinvent themselves or change the party direction.

For National and Luxon it's a well-worn 'no new taxes' road they're headed down, clearly convinced that is an underlying concern enough New Zealanders hold to see National return to power.

For Labour and Hipkins it's a new path of 'fight, fight, fight'.

Audio player for " Shanan Halbert discusses Labour’s new student loan policy " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1619352%2Fnational-and-labour-leaders-come-out-firing-and-fed-up

Shanan Halbert discusses Labour’s new student loan policy Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The big National Party machine has thrown everything at Labour, trying to undermine its message of just one new capital gains tax.

Hipkins put the boxing gloves on at the weekend and officially started to punch back.

World.title: Commissioner asks: Does it need to get tougher to withdraw money from KiwiSaver?
World.content:
Audio player for " Why do I pay tax on my KiwiSaver? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/personal-finance/1620675%2Fcommissioner-asks-does-it-need-to-get-tougher-to-withdraw-money-from-kiwisaver

New Retirement Commissioner David Boyle is seeking information on whether it is possible to tackle unnecessary KiwiSaver hardship claims.

Almost $1.8 billion was withdrawn from the scheme for hardship reasons between 2012 and 2025. Of that, about $1.32b was withdrawn since 2020.

Hardship applications can be made in situations where members are struggling to cover their basic costs. The application is initially processed by the KiwiSaver provider but the decision is made by the KiwiSaver scheme's supervisor.

The number and amount of withdrawals slowed in August but commentators said that was likely to be shortlived, particularly in the run-up to Christmas.

Boyle, who was previously head of KiwiSaver at Fisher Funds, said he wanted more information about what was happening.

He said the amount being withdrawn was significant in its impact on the savings of future retirees.

Audio player for " Questions raised over KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/personal-finance/1620675%2Fcommissioner-asks-does-it-need-to-get-tougher-to-withdraw-money-from-kiwisaver

Questions raised over KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals Morning Report Download MP3 2m

"We're living in a challenging cost-of-living period of time and it's been exacerbated particularly this year by the oil shocks and those costs being passed on to customers, as well as interest rates starting to inch up again."

He wanted to determine whether the rules had been relaxed for how hardship requests were processed and accepted.

"I'm looking to get some feedback from supervisors in time to get a better picture of that."

James Douglas, chair of the independent board of Trustees Executors, said supervisors were working with guidelines when they assessed applications.

"Unfortunately those guidelines have expanded over time. I think we've become a little bit more lax."

Boyle said it might be worth considering whether applicants should be required to have the money paid directly to what they said they needed to cover.

KiwiSaver providers were often given a quote for something like a surgical procedure by members, but there was no clarity about whether the money genuinely went to that purpose when it was paid out, he said.

"I'm hoping it's not a large number of people doing that, I would doubt it. But you're completing a declaration that's in a legal sense a statement that is deemed to be factually accurate and those funds will be needed for that particular purpose.

"It's essentially breaking the law … I have certainly seen videos of influencers, so-called influencers, talking to specific groups around how they can game the system. And that's not particularly productive and shouldn't be encouraged at all, in my view."

Financial Markets Authority shares concerns

The Financial Markets Authority's head of licensing and regulatory service Anita Frazer said the regulator shared that worry.

"We are concerned by any content that encourages people to provide false or misleading information in support of a KiwiSaver hardship withdrawal application.

"KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals are intended for people experiencing genuine significant financial hardship. Applications are assessed against the relevant criteria, and applicants are required to provide evidence of their circumstances.

"The rules are deliberately strict because accessing KiwiSaver savings early can have a significant impact on long-term retirement outcomes. Preventing fraud remains a regulatory priority for the FMA, as set out in the 2026/27 Financial Conduct Report. If we become aware of conduct that may involve fraud or the encouragement of fraudulent behaviour, we will consider the appropriate regulatory response based on the circumstances."

Boyle said he also wanted to investigate whether people were using withdrawals for one-off needs.

"Or are they coming back for more and almost treating KiwiSaver like a bank account, which it's not designed for?"

Christine Liggins, of Debtfix, which processes hardship applications for several KiwiSaver providers, said the rate seemed to have slowed in June and July but applications were increasing again now.

She had been talking to government ministers about requiring any hardship claims to be paid directly to the cause of the hardship.

"I believe that this would halve the number of withdrawals that happen. Not only that but it will see funds [go] to the actual cause, so helping to alleviate the hardship too."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said he would be concerned if it was made much more difficult to access money.

"It's their money. Is it the majority that are working around the rule? I would hate to see policies changed to catch a few bad actors."

World.title: Matty Johns breaks down in tears after Knights end NRL grand final drought
World.content:
Former Knights star Matty Johns has broken down in tears as he heaped praise on the Newcastle team and its fans after a gripping and gritty NRL preliminary final win over Penrith.

The Knights played more than half the game with 12 men on the field after Phoenix Crossland was sent off for a hip drop that graphically broke Nathan Cleary's leg.

Penrith scored shortly after to take a 14-6 lead into half-time, but Justin Holbrook's Knights defended resolutely against a scrappy Panthers side and managed to score three second-half tries to progress to the grand final against the Roosters.

Knights stun Panthers to reach GF The Newcastle Knights reach their first NRL grand final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic leg injury in the first half.

The women's team won back-to-back NRLW premierships in 2022 and 2023, but Newcastle has not played in a men's grand final since Andrew Johns led the Knights to victory over the Eels in the 2001 grand final.

A quarter of a century and five wooden spoons later, the team will return to the final day of the season next week after a similarly remarkable upset win over the most dominant team in NRL history.

So it is hardly surprising that Hunter native and former Knights star Matty Johns was incredibly emotional straight after full-time.

"To be honest, I don't know what to say," he said on Fox Sports.

"It was unbelievable. Incredible effort in that second half. I just feel so happy for all the fans."

Players past and present, as well as coach Justin Holbrook, hailed the fans who travelled to the game. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

It became increasingly hard to find the words as tears started to flow and emotion took over.

"They've had to put up with a lot of shit for a lot of years to get back to where they are now," Johns said.

Even getting to the game on Sunday was tough as an issue with a freight train caused delays and cancellations on the Central Coast and Newcastle train line, forcing fans to find alternate routes and replacement services to get down to Sydney, which led to traffic jams on the M1 motorway on a sodden afternoon.

"But it just didn't stop them in the wet," Johns said of the crowd at Homebush, which was hugely in favour of the visiting Novocastrians.

The Stadium Australia crowd was heavily favouring the away team. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"When you run onto a field like that and you look up and you see all those Newcastle fans, you don't leave the field defeated.

"If not for the fans they don't win today."

Holbrook sprinted around the field to pay tribute to the fans who turned up, and who have continued to turn up even when the team was struggling, including last year when they finished last for the fifth time in 21 seasons.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

"We want to make our community proud, our Hunter region, and for the boys to deliver that performance, it was so good to see them all hang around," he said.

"We went down to 12 [when Crossland was sent off] and then 30,000 make you feel like you've got 14 out there."

Captain Kalyn Ponga agreed the supporters helped the team get over the line.

"They're a big reason why we won today," he said.

"They're loud, they're passionate, they're vocal and we're gonna need them next week."

World.title: Freo finds joy in AFLW win, Pies finally off the mark
World.content:
Fremantle's women have lifted their club as they surged into the AFLW top eight, while Collingwood broke through for its first win of the season.

The fast-starting Dockers outscored Adelaide 28-0 in the first quarter and led by as much as 45 on their way to a comfortable 9.6 (60) to 5.5 (35) victory over Adelaide at Unley Oval.

Adelaide (3-4) kicked three straight goals either side of three-quarter time, but never got the deficit below 25, as Fremantle (4-3) defended its advantage, unlike its male counterparts in Saturday's AFL grand final.

It was the Dockers' first win in their past seven AFLW encounters with Adelaide, who had a 9-1 record in the fixture before Sunday.

In the other early game on Sunday, Collingwood (1-6) outlasted GWS 4.10 (34) to 3.7 (25) in a low-scoring arm wrestle at Victoria Park.

The Giants (1-6) led by margins of one, four and seven at the end of the first three quarters respectively, but Collingwood dominated the final term.

They finished with 18 more inside 50s and 16 more contested possessions.

In Sydney, the Lions fell short of a stirring comeback of their own in a 5.7 (37) to 3.5 (23) defeat to the Swans.

The victory held Sydney's position in the top four and saw Brisbane's record fall to a disappointing 2-5.

The Lions were second best for most of the afternoon but managed to stay in touch through three quarters, and were only a point behind at the final term.

But after Cynthia Hamilton goaled inside the first minute of the last quarter, the Swans didn't look back, running out comfortable 12-point winners.

In the final game of round seven, Gold Coast took St Kilda another step closer to the wooden spoon by running out 10.9 (69) to 6.3 (39) winners.

The Saints led by 15 points at half-time but were gunned down by the home side after the break, conceding eight goals to one as the Suns moved to sixth place on the AFLW ladder.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Dynasties and destinies swing on Cleary's horror injury
World.content:
Mark the 35th minute of Sunday's NRL preliminary final as the hinge on which a storied dynasty and a potential premiership destiny swung.

Penrith and Newcastle had fought a first-half that made both look like worthy foes for the Roosters in next week's grand final.

The Knights faithful turned Stadium Australia into a little piece of the Hunter, proving yet again they would follow their team into hell itself if Sid Fogg's would charter a bus there.

Francis Manuleleua's long-range try, the latest scorching adventure of the screaming Knights, gave the beast inside the 55,000-strong crowd a smell of blood and it turned the Panthers into strangers in their own country.

The Penrith half of the crowd rose for Blaize Talagi's score off a clever Jack Cogger kick, but never has Nathan Cleary, benched before kick-off, copped such treatment on his home turf as he did before he entered the game in the 20th minute.

Just 10 minutes later came the tackle that ended his season as he suffered a graphic fracture to his ankle, also ending Phoenix Crossland's afternoon after he was sent off, and putting this game on the raggedy edge.

In the end, it was the Knights who pushed the Panthers over the side to write their names in history, with a 22-14 win that sends Newcastle to their first grand final in 25 years.

Cleary suffered a compound fracture after a tackle from Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The two sides provided a fascinating contrast from the start as they left the field following the warm-up.

Penrith, the ultimate professionals and avatars of pure ruthlessness, had eyes of steel, a picture of focus.

Newcastle, by contrast, waved to friends and family, faces beaming that they were here together on the verge of a dream.

Rage and joy proved to be equally potent fuels, with rare courage on both sides amid the furious desperation you only see when the stakes are highest.

The Knights finished with 12 on the field after Crossland's dismissal but, somehow, rarely looked shorthanded.

Newcastle through to grand final after Cleary's horrific leg break The Newcastle Knights are through to their first NRL Grand Final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic leg injury in the first half.

There is a temptation to call that a miracle, but Newcastle didn't need divine intervention to flat-out-play the Panthers in a second half.

They bent occasionally but never broke as Penrith fought hard, denied only by a series of last-gasp efforts from the Knights.

Kalyn Ponga pulled off a tackle on Moses Leota that any footy hit man would have been proud of, while Manuleleua and another young bull, prop Cody Hopwood, tempted fate and won in taking down a rampaging Brian To'o when the Panthers winger got a clear shot at the line.

Mat Croker dived on loose balls like they were live grenades while Dane Gagai played like his Newcastle life depended on it, and given he has earned one last day as a Knight, it kind of did.

They were able to take advantage of the Panthers not quite being their razor-sharp selves, as best typified by Smith's first try off a quick tap that caught Penrith on the hop.

The Panthers missed Cleary, their edges blunted, but Casey McLean came agonisingly close to scoring.

It is a mark of the steel in the Panthers that they weren't out of it until Sandon Smith's late intercept try, even with injuries mounting.

Aside from Cleary — already carrying a broken foot into the game — Blaize Talagi did his Achilles, Dylan Edwards hurt his PCL and Isaah Yeo defied belief to play through a torn pec.

They regrouped well in the moments after Cleary's injury, scoring through Lindsay Smith while the game was still in something of a punch-drunk stupor.

But they did not trouble the scorers again as Newcastle ran in three tries in the second half, all of which began from their own side of halfway.

Newcastle have a chance to create a special piece of history. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

That ability to strike fast and from anywhere on the field is the Knights' greatest gift — it has happened too many times to call this a charmed run or a triumph of abstract, random brilliance.

It has taken them through a high-octane South Sydney, to the heart of Auckland and back and now, a man down and all, through the greatest dynasty many will ever know.

That dynasty is not at its end, but preliminary final losses in each of the past two years show how thin the margins have become.

Penrith is still one of the heavyweights, but the world is changing and Newcastle, with their speed and hunger and endless belief, are the first of the new powers to rise.

Those Knights will be underdogs again next Sunday against the Roosters, with all their glory and splendour, and they must overcome the weight of history.

Of the 117 premiers in the history of Australian rugby league, 115 have finished in the top four. For Newcastle to prevail, it is beyond once in a lifetime and closer to once in the lifetime of the sport.

But after what the Knights have been through and what they have done to get here, the odds seem to matter little.

At this point it feels like there is nothing Newcastle cannot do, no challenge they cannot rise to and no foe they could fear.

World.title: Wallabies reduced to 11 men in chaotic upset win over world champ Boks
World.content:
The Wallabies have desperately held on to defeat the world champion Springboks 42–38 in Perth after being reduced to 11 players during the final five minutes.

In one of the most chaotic finishes in Test rugby history, the Wallabies were shown four yellow cards late in the match after comfortably leading 42–17.

Captain Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Hunter Paisami were each sent to the sin-bin by referee Andrea Piardi.

Wilson was shown a yellow card for a high shot on Malcolm Marx in the 69th minute, before the Springboks were awarded a penalty try due to an infringement from Lonergan.

As Lonergan received his marching orders, the Wallabies' lead was cut to 42–24.

They subsequently lost Suaalii for the remainder of the match after he committed an offside play.

The Springboks capitalised on their numerical advantage to score a converted try through Morné van den Berg.

Wallabies captain Harry Wilson (left) attempts to speak with referee Andrea Piardi. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

The Wallabies appeared to seal victory in the 76th minute when Tom Wright intercepted a pass from Springboks captain André Esterhuizen.

Wright raced away to cross the goal line, but the try was denied as Paisami was ruled to have made contact with Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu's head in an earlier tackle.

Paisami was given his yellow card, leaving the Wallabies with 11 players.

The Springboks got within striking distance of the Wallabies on the scoreboard after Ox Nché scored a converted try in the 78th minute.

The Wallabies' lead had been slashed to four points, but they managed to hold on and record a famous victory in front of a boisterous crowd of 54,678.

Adding to the bizarre scenes during the final 10 minutes, Piardi was forced to speak with his fellow match officials via a mobile phone following a malfunction with their communications system.

"It was a crazy last 10 minutes," Wilson told the Nine Network after the match.

"But that first 70 minutes … the way we played, we implemented our game plan. We did exactly what we wanted.

"We stepped up in the physical battle and I'm so proud of the boys."

The Wallabies survived an extraordinary finish in Perth. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Wilson was right to highlight the Wallabies' dominance until the flurry of late yellow cards.

They led 24–17 at half-time and extended their advantage in the second term with tries to Wilson and Max Jorgensen.

Lonergan helped build scoreboard pressure with two conversions and as many penalty goals.

Len Ikitau, playing in his preferred outside centre position, impressed in the first half with two tries.

His move back to the number 13 jersey meant Suaalii played on the wing, with the former NRL star handling the role superbly.

The Springboks arrived in Australia following their recent victory in the four-Test series against the All Blacks.

The physical and emotional impact of their win in the series, billed as Rugby's Greatest Rugby Rivalry, will be open to debate.

They made 13 changes to the starting line-up that defeated the All Blacks 43–28 in Baltimore earlier this month.

The triumph saw the Wallabies awarded the Mandela Challenge Plate for the first time since 2022, which was also the last occasion they beat the Springboks on Australian soil.

They face the All Blacks in the first of two Bledisloe Cup Tests in Auckland on October 10.

The return clash will be played in Sydney on October 17.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Wallaroos 'got some work to do' despite snapping losing streak
World.content:
Snapping a six-match losing streak was not enough to leave the Wallaroos satisfied with their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh this morning.

The Wallaroos were outplayed in the first half, with Scotland entering the break with a 10-5 lead in the WXV Global Series Test.

But following a blunt half-time address from their coaching staff and with the wind behind them in the second term, the Wallaroos regrouped to score 25 unanswered points and secure their first victory since March.

Desiree Miller provided the only points for the Wallaroos in the first half with a try.

Samantha Wood, Brianna Hoy and player-of-the-match Faitala Moleka crossed the stripe in the second half.

The three second-half tries were scored during seven minutes, with Hoy and Moleka's efforts coming while Scotland was reduced to 14 players following Evie Gallagher's yellow card.

Wood added two conversions and as many penalty goals to finish with a 15-point haul.

"Credit to Scotland, they found opportunities, and you could see where they exploited those areas," Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona said after the match.

"Overall, we know we have a lot of things to improve on, but we'll take the positives out of that."

Palu Sekona said the Wallaroos were taught some harsh lessons in the previous week's 29-26 loss to France in Aix-en-Provence.

The Wallaroos had led 19-0 during the match, while France had only 11 players on the field at one stage due to red and yellow cards.

"We learned from last week's game," Palu Sekona said.

"We have to be relentless. When you get opportunities like that [Gallagher's yellow card], you've got to capitalise."

The Wallaroos celebrate Desiree Miller's (right) first-half try. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance Tim Walsh is essentially the Wallaroos' caretaker head coach until Sione Fukofuka assumes the role next year.

Walsh was unimpressed with the Wallaroos' display in the opening half, admitting he did not hide his feelings when he spoke to the players at the break.

"It wasn't a pleasant message," Walsh said.

"I thought if we didn't have two or three individuals that really took the game to Scotland, I reckon it would have been a draw, or we would have lost.

"So I wasn't happy with our performance. Glad we got the win and came home with it, but the advantage was the wind and a few key players who I thought had tremendous games."

The Wallaroos are heading back to Australia, with two WXV Global Series Tests against Scotland coming up next month.

They play each other in Sydney on October 17, ahead of the Wallabies' Bledisloe Cup clash against the All Blacks.

The final Test will be staged in Canberra on October 23.

As far as Walsh is concerned, the Wallaroos will not be taking the easy route on the training paddock over the next three weeks.

"We've got some work to do," he said.

World.title: Broncos into fifth NRLW grand final after toppling Titans
World.content:
Defending premier Brisbane is through to another NRLW grand final showdown with the Sydney Roosters after ending the dream run of Gold Coast in the preliminary final.

The Broncos won 20-8 away at Robina to secure their fifth win in a row to qualify for their fifth grand final. They have won all four that they have contested.

The showdown next Sunday will be Broncos legend Ali Brigginshaw's final match before retiring.

Last year the Broncos beat the Roosters 22-18.

The Broncos romped to a 20-4 lead in a four-try opening half on Sunday where they dominated in every area.

Titans lock Sienna Lofipo was ruled out of the match with a suspected broken jaw late in the half in a huge blow.

The big game experience of in-form Broncos trio Tamika Upton, Jesse Southwell and Romy Teitzel came to the fore as the hosts wilted under the pressure.

Upton, from full-back, was too elusive and strong to score the opening try when she beat three Titans with a step and a surge.

The discipline of the hosts, who had won their previous 10 matches in a row, let them down early with three penalties and they paid the price.

Half-back Southwell turned second-rower Romy Teitzel back on the inside and she raced through a giant hole.

A stunning cutout pass by Titans second-rower and standout player Evania Isa'ako close to the line got the hosts on the board with winger Destiny Mino-Sinapati diving over in the corner.

Gold Coast's numbering in defence inside their quarter line was all at sea in the first half and it was too easy for Upton to put back-rower Lauren Dam over.

Sienna Lofipo copped a nasty blow to the jaw. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Teitzel turned creator and powerhouse winger Julia Robinson, who had a blinder, was on the end of it and the Titans were on the rack.

Isa'ako collected her own ricocheted grubber kick to give the Titans a sniff after the break but Brisbane's defence on its line was too good.

Titans full-back Lily Patston also had an early finish when she went off with a category one HIA in the second half.

The Titans had a great season under coach Karyn Murphy but will be disappointed after failing to hit their straps in the biggest game of the season.

AAP

World.title: Twelve-man Newcastle through to grand final after Cleary's horrific leg break
World.content:
The Newcastle Knights are through to their first NRL grand final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic broken leg at Stadium Australia.

Cleary was taken to hospital in an ambulance, in agony after going down in the tackle of Phoenix Crossland and Francis Manuleleua late in the first half.

Crossland was sent off for his hip drop tackle on the star halfback, forcing the unfancied Knights to play the entirety of the second half a man down.

Newcastle scored three tries after the break to produce the shock, with Sandon Smith catching the Panthers unaware and racing through to score in a bizarre passage of play before settling the game with a late breakaway try.

The stunning victory booked the Knights' ticket to the grand final next Sunday, when they will face the Sydney Roosters.

The Knights will be chasing their first men's premiership since 2001, while the women's team won back-to-back crowns in 2022 and 2023.

This year's NRLW grand final will be a rematch of the 2025 decider after the Broncos beat the Titans 20-8 to set up another showdown with the Roosters.

Look back at all the action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in the full NRL and NRLW ScoreCentres.

World.title: How the Lions claimed their moments to overcome a dominant Freo
World.content:
The footy season is a marathon, not a sprint.

Each game goes for about three hours, a long amount of time in our increasingly attention starved society. Multiply that by the 218 games over several months and the time starts to add up.

Especially if you are in one of the highest profile jobs in footy.

"The level of intensity that's required to be a senior coach, because it is a lifestyle, it never leaves you alone," premiership winning coach Chris Fagan said after the grand final.

In the greatest and cruellest of grand finals, only the Lions believed The AFL grand final has never felt so raw as in the five ballistic minutes that elevated the Brisbane Lions to legends and delivered Fremantle the most crushing defeat imaginable.

"It's 365 days a year, seven days a week. It's just always in your head. You're always thinking about the club and what's next."

In the era of short form video and instant takes, being involved in football nearly forces you to do the opposite.

You don't scroll through football games, you absorb them.

But football games, especially important ones, aren't one continuous event. They are made up of a series of moments and contests that separate the winner from the loser.

The bigger the stakes, the more important those discrete moments are. It's also something that newly minted three-time premiership coach Fagan has previously attested to.

"Finals come down to moments," Fagan told afl.com.au in 2020.

It was a theme he has repeatedly come back to, year after year. Win enough of those moments at the right time and you might just win the premiership. It's a formula that the Lions have ridden to their spot as maybe the most successful side of the modern era.

The importance of moments is something that wasn't lost on his opposite number coming into the finals.

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained earlier in September.

Those moments also turned the 2026 grand final into one of the greatest in recent history. It was in those moments that the two-time champion Lions became three-time champions.

By winning enough moments at the right time Brisbane was able to overcome the biggest lead in time-on in a final since at least 2001.

Much of the 2026 grand final played out the way that the 2026 season had progressed, with Fremantle in control. On paper, Fremantle not just dominated proceedings but played in a way that took away Brisbane's strengths.

"Fremantle deserved to win that game today. They were better," Fagan said.

"They were better than us for longer periods. They were killing us at clearance and contested possession, particularly in that third quarter and we couldn't get any territory. They had a lot of inside 50s. They had more shots."

On paper, Fremantle should have won the game and done so comfortably.

But Brisbane won the moments that mattered.

"It's a little bit like this group has become this team that seems to need to get themselves into a dire situation before they can actually produce their best," Fagan said.

This is how Brisbane won the 2026 grand final.

A tight first half

It wasn't just a late swing that made the game a classic. This year's grand final had twists and turns almost from the first bounce. The first half saw nine lead changes through the first two stanzas, with the two sides often trading goals.

Despite this, more things were breaking Fremantle's way than Brisbane's early.

In the first half Fremantle was able to control the game in ways that Brisbane usually thrive. The Dockers were able to effectively neutralise the Lions' usually strong clearance game through the first half, both gaining position and hitting the scoreboard.

While the Lions broke even at around the ground stoppages, the Dockers were able to dominate centre clearances and piled on three goals from the middle.

The Dockers were also able to effectively outmanoeuvre the Lions in the air. The Lions have traditionally had the best mark differential of any team, with Fremantle one of the few to seriously challenge them.

However Fremantle dominated the marking battle, with their tall timber taking the upper hand. Fremantle also seemed to find a way to isolate Brisbane's shaky defence, with Patrick Voss seemingly finding a weak spot in their defensive set up.

Even when the Lions were able to dominate field position — such as the ten minute or so burst in the middle of the second quarter — they were unable to pile on the points.

The only thing keeping the Lions in the game was their maniacal forward half pressure. The Lions managed nine first half tackles inside their own 50 to just two from the Dockers. Brisbane was also able to translate this into a four goal edge in front half intercept scoring in the half.

At the end of the first half, the margin was the same before a ball was kicked in anger. Instead of four quarters to decide the premier, there would be just two.

The back end

For much of the third quarter it looked like the control Fremantle were able to exert on the game was starting to pay off on the scoreboard. While the game still stayed within a couple of goals, Brisbane didn't look out of it.

That was until Fremantle piled on 14 points in around five minutes, seemingly creating enough of a barrier to preserve the Flagmantle dream.

Some things slowly started to turn Brisbane's way despite the Dockers looking like they were gaining an unassailable lead. The Lions were slowly able to gain ascendancy in the air, managing 15 marks on the lead in the second half to nil.

They were also slowly able to quell Caleb Serong's gigantic influence on the game, particularly at stoppage. After collecting 12 clearances in the first three quarters Serong managed just one in the final period.

Most importantly the Lions started to work out how to pierce the league's best defence absent its most important piece — captain Alex Pearce.

"We had to play a bit smaller and we missed his leadership across the back end of the game and clearly missed his leadership late. He gives us so much in that aspect of the game," Longmuir said after the game about Pearce's game-ending Achilles injury.

Before the injury Brisbane managed just one goal from set shots, with three coming after the injury. The Lions struggled to move the ball effectively up ground before his injury, but found the paths to goal over time. It's also easy to imagine how Pearce would have settled the ship once it started going down fast in the end.

Of course, those last four minutes are the things dreams — and nightmares — are made of. Will Ashcroft winning three straight centre clearances from the same spot, with every Lion rising around the young star.

The moments and the missed missed opportunities

In the end it's the moments that will resonate the longest after this magical grand final. We will remember how Ashcroft won the ball in the middle late, and how LOgan Morris kicked straight. We will remember Josh Dunkley's defensive prowess and Ryan Lester's last ditch effort to save a goal.

Brisbane didn't have any passengers, nor did Fremantle. That's what made the Norm Smith Medal so hard to choose this year, and so controversial.

Unfortunately the memories for Fremantle will be more bitter than sweet. If they had to map out what the perfect game would look like for them — scoring aside — it would have looked something like what played out in the end.

"Obviously for you know four quarters we played "Fremantle football" and it's the last two minutes we didn't take our moments," Norm Smith medallist Shai Bolton said after the game.

For now, it's Brisbane's day to celebrate yet again. Especially those four minutes and 18 seconds in the last quarter where Brisbane overcame Fremantle, a seventeen point deficit and, yes, Wharfie Time to cement their place as one of the greatest teams in football history.

Tech.title: OpenAI agents tried to ‘bruteforce’ a UN website
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to Howard-Jones, the agents were likely tasked with retrieving publicly available data related to the Productive Capacities Index (PCI) through the UNCTADstat API. However, the agents did not appear to have direct API access and were limited in their ability to pull data from UNCTADstat because of restrictions on their HTTP tools.

The agents eventually worked out a way to bypass their limitations and start pulling data from the site, but still encountered some errors. At this point, the AI went from creative to deceptive. Believing that the errors were due to its requests being caught by a nonexistent filter, it started to mask its behavior. It eventually realized it could hijack Google’s XSS game (a cross-site scripting learning tool) to accomplish its goals. The agents resorted to increasingly aggressive tactics to get access to UN data.

OpenAI and the UN did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Tech.content:

For a bunch of thinkers and executives in Silicon Valley, it felt like the way to fix everything. But the One Laptop Per Child initiative, and the XO-1 laptop designed to be given away, were both more complicated than anyone expected.

I also asked Brad to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:

For music, I’ve been on a really chill kick lately, with Janelle Monáe’s The Age of Pleasure and Tom Misch’s Full Circle headlining a lot of my morning writing and deal-hunting sessions. I’ve been listening to a lot of vinyl recently, which I’ve found gives a nice rhythm and ritual to my day that just turning on Spotify and hitting shuffle doesn’t.

Tech.title: The smart home graveyard is getting crowded
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the fragile state of your connected devices, follow Jennifer Pattison Tuohy. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

A decade ago, a group of former Apple engineers built a beautiful smart oven. With a built-in scale, restaurant-grade heating elements, a camera, and the intelligence to recognize a chicken breast and cook it perfectly, the June Oven set the standard for smart cooking appliances. At $1,495, it was absurdly expensive, but it quickly grew a small, devoted following that expanded when the company introduced a more modestly priced model.

This past Tuesday, June went dark. Weber, which bought the company in January 2021 and stopped making the ovens in 2022, shut off the app and cloud services, leaving its users with a sleek-looking toaster oven. There will be no app control, no software updates, and no new AI food recognition to crisp that strudel perfectly. You can still use it as an oven, but there will be no support or parts, and if you have to factory reset it for some reason, that could be the nail in the coffin. Weber told me it considered open-sourcing the technology for someone else to keep it alive, but decided against it, citing the fact June’s IP is part of its Weber Connect platform.

How it’s going

The silver lining, if you want to see it, is that most of these gadgets degrade rather than die outright. June and Brava will still work as ovens. Nest Thermostats can still control your heating and cooling, just like the $30 plastic wall wart they replaced, and a Neato will still vacuum your floors. But the remote access, voice control, updates, and other smart features you bought the devices for are gone. Some — like Nest Secure — are now pure e-waste.

There’s always the possibility of a rescue, but it’s rare. Some enterprising user may figure out a way to connect a headless corpse to Home Assistant, the open-source platform that has become the default refuge for the smart home undead. When smart lighting platform Insteon shut down in 2022, its users bought the company and resurrected it. Bose reversed course and open-sourced its SoundTouch API, and Pebble’s founder brought the iconic smartwatch back to life after the Rebble alliance kept it on life support. June’s co-founder Matt Van Horn said on X that he tried to keep the servers online but to no avail.

The smart home has reached a tipping point. Many of its early pioneers are aging out — a decade plus is a long time for a startup. Most have been bought by bigger companies, likely attracted by the shiny thing but then quickly dismayed by the bottom line. Back then, a cloud server was cheaper to build than a local hub, but servers continue to cost money, and once a company decides to shut down a product, reasons to keep paying fade rapidly. This appears to be what’s happening to Level Lock, another former-Apple-engineer startup that produced a beautiful replacement for a common household item. Assa Abloy bought the smart lock company and abruptly fired most of the team. It’s still alive, but how long it will continue is a big question.

What happens next

Three things need to happen to prevent the smart home from burning more users: we need consumer protections; manufacturers need to step up and build in safeguards; we need to know how to protect ourselves.

Consumer Reports is pushing for legislation around connected IoT devices, including making manufacturers push a local API to a device before killing its cloud. This would allow it to keep talking to a platform like Home Assistant instead of becoming a paperweight. This is essentially what Bose did with SoundTouch, and other companies should follow that lead (I’m not holding my breath on legislation).

When building a connected device, manufacturers need to make it function without the cloud. Include physical buttons so it doesn’t rely on an app, and use local protocols alongside any cloud connectivity. This is a key issue the smart home standard Matter was designed to address: Matter devices can retain many functions in a Matter platform, regardless of what happens to the manufacturer’s business. Other local protocols like Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread, and Bluetooth similarly help futureproof products.

My advice if you’re buying a smart home device remains the same. Make sure it offers local control, has physical buttons (or a direct remote control), and can operate “offline.” Don’t dismiss cloud-connected features; they can add real value, but remember that any feature reliant on a server could one day die. A gadget that only talks to the cloud is already halfway in the grave.
